records.Subject: Civil Law
records.Topic: Persons and Family Relations — Void Marriages as a Defense to Bigamy
records.Essay Question: In 1981, JR married then 16-year-old Inka in a civil ceremony solemnized by the Mayor in their hometown. The couple lived together until 2007 when JR confessed to having an affair with Elena. Inka later discovered that JR and Elena got married in 1995. Inka thus filed a criminal complaint against JR for Bigamy. In his defense, JR insisted that he could not be held criminally liable for Bigamy because his marriage with Inka in 1981 is void for lack of a valid marriage license, while his marriage with Elena is void for lack of a marriage ceremony. Meanwhile, Elena claimed that even prior to the Bigamy case, she already filed a petition for nullity of marriage before the Regional Trial Court (RTC) of Quezon City sometime in 2007 after learning about the marriage between JR and Inka. The RTC later declared the marriage of JR and Elena as void for being bigamous, and the ruling attained finality due to lack of appeal. Does JR have a valid defense in the Bigamy case? Decide with reasons.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes, conditionally. JR has a valid defense if he proves that the first marriage was void ab initio for lack of a valid marriage license, or that the second marriage was independently void ab initio for lack of a marriage ceremony. The judgment declaring the second marriage void merely because it was bigamous does not, standing alone, exculpate him.

Legal Basis: Article 349 of the Revised Penal Code requires a subsisting first marriage and a subsequent marriage possessing the essential requisites for validity. Under Articles 2, 3, 4, and 35 of the Family Code, absence of an essential or formal requisite—subject to statutory exceptions—renders a marriage void. In Pulido v. People, the Supreme Court held that an accused may prove in the bigamy case that the prior or subsequent marriage was void ab initio; a prior judicial declaration of nullity is not indispensable for that defense.

Application: If JR proves that no valid marriage license supported the first marriage and no license exception applied, the prosecution cannot establish a legally subsisting first marriage. Alternatively, if he proves that no marriage ceremony occurred for the second union, that union lacked an essential requisite of marriage. Either independently proven defect may defeat an element of bigamy. However, the later declaration that the second marriage was void because it was bigamous only follows from the alleged bigamy and cannot by itself erase criminal liability.

Conclusion: JR has a valid defense only upon proof of an independent void-ab-initio ground affecting the first or second marriage; the bigamy-based nullity judgment alone is insufficient.

records.Subject: Civil Law
records.Topic: Persons and Family Relations — Custody of an Illegitimate Child
records.Essay Question: Anita is an entertainer in Empyrea, a men’s club and lounge. One evening, Billy, the exclusive patron of Anita, asked her out on a date outside of Empyrea. After spending the night together, Billy got Anita pregnant. A year after giving birth to Marisol and despite the vehement opposition of Billy, Anita went back to her previous job in Empyrea to support her child. Anita was able to provide a house, a nanny, and other necessities for Marisol. Billy, however, insisted that Anita no longer needed to work if she and Marisol stayed with him as he could provide for them. Since Anita refused to live with Billy, the latter filed a petition for custody of Marisol. Anita contended that illegitimate children are automatically under the sole custody and parental authority of the mother. On the other hand, Billy alleged that Anita is unfit to take care of Marisol given her line of work. If you are the judge, how will you decide the petition? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: The petition should be denied, and custody should remain with Anita.

Legal Basis: Article 176 of the Family Code places an illegitimate child under the parental authority of the mother. Article 213 provides that a child below seven years of age should not be separated from the mother absent compelling reasons. Pablo-Gualberto v. Gualberto V teaches that the child’s best interests are paramount and that alleged moral lapses justify removing custody only when they adversely affect the child’s welfare or materially impair proper parental care.

Application: Marisol is an illegitimate young child, and Anita has supplied a home, care, and necessities. Billy relies on Anita’s work at a men’s club, but the occupation alone does not establish an imperative or compelling cause, nor does it show harm to Marisol or neglect of parental duties. On the stated facts, transferring custody would displace the statutory maternal authority without proof of unfitness.

Conclusion: Billy’s petition should be denied because Marisol’s best interests and the governing custody rules favor Anita.

records.Subject: Civil Law
records.Topic: Property and Succession — Sale of a Co-owner’s Undivided Share
records.Essay Question: Lani and Rufino died leaving four children, two of whom are Arturo and Bugoy. The heirs signed a document selling half of the property of their parents to their friend, Honorato. One of the remaining quarters was occupied by Ildefonso and Bienvenido, the children of Arturo, while the other quarter was sold by Bugoy to the Spouses Cruz by virtue of a deed of sale. Shortly after, the Spouses Cruz filed an ejectment case against Ildefonso and Bienvenido for the 1/4 portion of the subject property that they purchased. On the other hand, Bienvenido filed a complaint for recovery of ownership, quieting of title, and annulment of deed of sale against the Spouses Cruz. He alleged that the deed of sale is void since Bugoy is not the true and real owner of the subject property, which originally belonged to the estate of Rufino. On the other hand, the Spouses Cruz argued that Bienvenido availed of the wrong remedy, and claimed that the heirs had already agreed to divide the property among themselves when they allowed a portion of the property to be occupied by the heirs of Arturo. Will the complaint of Bienvenido prosper? Discuss.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No, the complaint will not prosper insofar as it seeks to nullify the sale outright or recover the common property from the buyers. The conveyance is effective at least to the extent of Bugoy’s undivided share, subject to partition.

Legal Basis: Under the Civil Code rules on co-ownership, each co-owner has full ownership of his or her undivided share and may alienate it, but the effect of an alienation involving a specific physical portion is limited to the portion ultimately allotted to the seller upon partition. Reyes v. Spouses Garcia holds that the buyer is substituted as co-owner to the extent of the seller’s pro-indiviso interest and that partition, rather than annulment of the sale or recovery of the common property, is the proper remedy for determining specific portions.

Application: Upon Lani’s and Rufino’s deaths, their children became co-owners before partition. Bugoy could therefore transfer his hereditary, undivided interest to the Spouses Cruz. Because the facts do not conclusively establish a binding partition, the sale does not necessarily give the buyers ownership of the exact physical quarter they claim; its effect is confined to whatever portion may be allotted to Bugoy. That uncertainty calls for partition, not total annulment of the deed.

Conclusion: Bienvenido’s action, as framed, should fail; the parties’ specific rights should be settled through partition, with the sale respected only within Bugoy’s lawful share.

records.Subject: Civil Law
records.Topic: Succession — Representation by Nonmarital Grandchildren
records.Essay Question: Felicia and Rocky met at a training convention and subsequently became lovers. They had children named Enrico and Euriz. One night while on his way home, Rocky met his end when his car collided with a speeding 15-wheeler truck along C-5 Road. A year later, the father of Rocky, Hilario, suffered a brain aneurysm and died. In the settlement of the estate of Hilario, Enrico and Euriz claimed an interest in the estate of their grandfather. They argued that as the biological children of Rocky, they are entitled to inherit from their grandparents by right of representation. The legitimate heirs of Hilario vehemently opposed the claim on the ground that Enrico and Euriz are barred from inheriting from the ascendants of Rocky. Are the legitimate heirs of Hilario correct? Explain your answer.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. On the stated facts, Enrico and Euriz may represent Rocky in Hilario’s estate, subject to proof of filiation and the ordinary requirements of intestate succession.

Legal Basis: Article 992 of the Civil Code contains the so-called iron-curtain rule, while the Code’s provisions on representation permit descendants to step into the place of a predeceased heir in the direct descending line. In Aquino v. Aquino, the Supreme Court reexamined Article 992 and held that nonmarital grandchildren are not barred from inheriting from their grandparents and other direct ascendants by right of representation solely because of their parents’ marital status.

Application: Rocky predeceased his father, Hilario. Enrico and Euriz are stated to be Rocky’s biological, nonmarital children. Their claim runs vertically through Rocky to their grandfather, not collaterally between the legitimate and nonmarital family lines that Article 992 was historically read to separate. Accordingly, once filiation and the other succession facts are established, they may occupy Rocky’s place by representation.

Conclusion: The legitimate heirs are incorrect; Article 992 does not, by itself, defeat Enrico’s and Euriz’s right to represent Rocky in Hilario’s estate.

records.Controlling Doctrine: Nonmarital grandchildren may inherit from grandparents and other direct ascendants by right of representation; Article 992 does not impose an iron curtain in the direct descending line solely because of marital status.

records.Subject: Civil Law
records.Topic: Damages — Temperate Damages for Unproved Funeral Expenses
records.Essay Question: Rene and Sebastian, who are bitter enemies, engaged in a gunfight. In the ensuing battle, Rene killed Sebastian with a shot to the head. In the criminal case for Murder filed against Rene, the heirs of Sebastian failed to establish funeral expenses due to the inadequacy of the evidence. Still, the trial court awarded temperate damages to the heirs, declaring that it cannot close its eyes to the fact that the heirs of Sebastian indeed incurred funeral expenses. Is the award proper? Discuss.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. An award of temperate damages is proper because the pecuniary loss is certain even though its exact amount was not adequately proved.

Legal Basis: Article 2224 of the Civil Code allows temperate or moderate damages when some pecuniary loss has been suffered but its amount cannot, from the nature of the case, be proved with certainty. Applying People v. Jugueta, the Supreme Court in People v. Badillo expressly recognized funeral and burial expenses as pecuniary losses supporting temperate damages when their exact amount was not proven.

Application: Sebastian’s death necessarily required disposition of his remains and caused his heirs to incur funeral or burial expenses. Their inadequate proof prevents an award of actual damages in an unverified amount, but it does not erase the established fact of pecuniary loss. Article 2224 therefore authorizes a reasonable temperate award.

Conclusion: The trial court properly awarded temperate damages despite the heirs’ failure to prove the exact funeral expenses.

records.Controlling Doctrine: Temperate damages may replace unproved actual funeral or burial expenses when death makes the pecuniary loss certain but the exact amount cannot be established.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Impossible Crime and Cybertheft
records.Essay Question: Taylor received Harry in her house and told him to feel at home. Inside the house, Harry planned to steal money from Taylor and covertly got hold of her cellphone. Harry tried to access Taylor’s electronic wallet account. After several attempts, Harry successfully opened Taylor’s electronic wallet but it has zero balance. Harry returned Taylor’s cellphone and left the house disappointed. Harry was charged with and convicted of impossible crime of theft. Is Harry liable for the impossible crime of theft? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. Harry is liable for an impossible crime involving cybertheft.

Legal Basis: Article 4(2) of the Revised Penal Code imposes liability when an act would be an offense against persons or property were it not for the inherent impossibility of accomplishment or the use of inadequate or ineffectual means. Laurel v. Abrogar holds that intangible property capable of appropriation may be the subject of theft. Section 6 of Republic Act No. 10175 increases the penalty when a Revised Penal Code crime is committed through information and communications technology.

Application: Harry intended to take money belonging to Taylor, obtained her phone, and accessed the electronic wallet. The intended taking failed only because the account unexpectedly contained no funds, a circumstance beyond his control. His acts would have constituted theft had the electronic funds existed, and he used information technology in executing them.

Conclusion: The inherent factual impossibility of taking money from the empty account makes him liable for the impossible crime, with the cybercrime qualifying circumstance.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Penal Code, Article 4(2); Republic Act No. 10175, Section 6; Laurel v. Abrogar, G.R. No. 155076, January 13, 2009: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/48437
records.Controlling Doctrine: An intended offense against property may constitute an impossible crime when completion is prevented by an unknown factual impossibility; intangible property can be the object of theft.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Laurel v. Abrogar

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Murder by Inducement; Reward and Treachery
records.Essay Question: Andy paid Billie PHP 50,000.00 to kill Charlie. Thereafter, Billie went to the house of Charlie and found him sound asleep. Billie took this opportunity and stabbed Charlie to death. The trial court convicted Andy and Billie of the crime of murder with aggravating circumstances of reward and treachery. Under Article 248 of the Revised Penal Code as amended by Republic Act No. 7659, the prescribed penalty for murder is reclusion perpetua to death. Considering that there are two aggravating circumstances, the trial court imposed upon Andy and Billie the penalty of reclusion perpetua without benefit of parole in lieu of death penalty in accordance with Republic Act No. 9346 or the law prohibiting the imposition of death penalty. Only Andy elevated the case to the Court of Appeals. Andy questioned the penalty and argued that he should only be liable for homicide with the prescribed penalty of reclusion temporal because the circumstances of reward and treachery cannot be appreciated against him. Decide what crime Andy committed and impose the proper penalty. Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Andy is guilty of murder as a principal by inducement, with reclusion perpetua as the proper penalty.

Legal Basis: Article 17 of the Revised Penal Code treats one who directly induces another to commit a crime as a principal. Under Article 248, a killing committed in consideration of a price, reward, or promise is murder. People v. Cañete holds that price or reward affects both the person who offers it and the person who accepts it. Under Article 62, a circumstance concerning the material execution, such as treachery, affects only a participant who knew of it.

Application: Andy’s payment was the determining inducement for Billie’s killing of Charlie, and the agreed reward itself qualified the killing as murder as to Andy. Nothing shows that Andy knew Billie would attack Charlie while asleep, so treachery cannot additionally aggravate Andy’s liability.

Conclusion: Andy is liable for murder by inducement, qualified by reward, and should be sentenced to reclusion perpetua.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Penal Code, Articles 17, 62, and 248; People v. Cañete, G.R. No. L-37945, May 28, 1984: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/assets/dtSearch/dtSearch_system_files/dtisapi6.dll?DocId=28275%26Index=%2A4aeb4dbdcceeda9b59b85ae3fb22cec0%26cmd=getdoc ; People v. Cabillan, G.R. No. 131808, February 6, 2002: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/50181
records.Controlling Doctrine: Price or reward qualifies the killing for both offeror and acceptor, while treachery affects an inducer only if the inducer knew the treacherous means would be used.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: People v. Cañete; People v. Cabillan

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Simple Theft Versus Qualified Theft
records.Essay Question: Adele, a grocery cashier, was charged under the following information which reads: “the accused with intent to gain and abuse of confidence feloniously stole grocery items worth PHP 1,500.00 without consent of her employer.” In due course, the trial court convicted Adele of qualified theft. The trial court ruled that Adele took advantage of her position as a cashier which entails high degree of confidence because it involves handling of the properties of the employer. Did the trial court properly convict Adele of qualified theft? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Adele should be liable only for simple theft on the stated facts.

Legal Basis: Article 308 of the Revised Penal Code defines theft. Under Article 310, theft is qualified by grave abuse of confidence only when the confidence reposed in the offender is substantial and the taking is facilitated by a serious breach of that trust. Batislaon v. People distinguishes mere employee access from the grave confidence required for qualified theft.

Application: Adele’s work gave her access to grocery items, but the facts do not show that those goods were specially entrusted to her custody or that a high fiduciary confidence, beyond ordinary employment access, enabled the taking.

Conclusion: The taking constitutes simple theft, not qualified theft.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Penal Code, Articles 308 and 310; Batislaon v. People, G.R. No. 256624, July 26, 2023: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/69203
records.Controlling Doctrine: Ordinary employee access does not by itself amount to the grave abuse of confidence required for qualified theft.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Attempted Sale of Dangerous Drugs
records.Essay Question: The police officers received confidential information that Larry was engaged in illegal drug trade activities. The authorities organized an entrapment operation and designated PO1 Miguel as poseur buyer. The operatives proceeded to the target area. The confidential informant introduced PO1 Miguel to Larry who intended to buy PHP 1,000.00-worth of shabu. Larry demanded payment but PO1 Miguel insisted that he should see the item first. Larry then took out a sachet from his pocket. PO1 Miguel wasted no time and executed the pre-arranged signal. The operatives rushed to the scene, arrested Larry, and seized the sachet. The confiscated item tested positive for shabu. Accordingly, Larry was charged with and convicted of illegal sale of dangerous drugs under Section 5 of Republic Act No. 9165 or the Comprehensive Dangerous Drugs Act of 2002. Larry appealed and argued that he is not criminally liable for illegal sale of dangerous drugs because there was no meeting of minds between him and PO1 Miguel as to the object and price of the transaction. Is Larry liable for violation of Republic Act No. 9165 even if the sale of dangerous drugs was not consummated? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. Larry is liable for attempted sale of dangerous drugs, which carries the same penalty prescribed for the consummated act under Republic Act No. 9165.

Legal Basis: Article 6 of the Revised Penal Code defines an attempt as commencement by overt acts without completion because of a cause other than spontaneous desistance. Section 26(b) of Republic Act No. 9165 punishes an attempt to sell dangerous drugs with the same penalty as the completed offense. People v. Tumulak applies these provisions where intent to sell and overt acts are proved but the sale is interrupted.

Application: Larry appeared for the transaction, demanded payment, possessed the shabu, and produced the sachet for the buyer. Police intervention prevented delivery and payment, not Larry’s voluntary desistance.

Conclusion: The facts establish attempted sale punishable under Sections 5 and 26(b) of Republic Act No. 9165.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Penal Code, Article 6; Republic Act No. 9165, Sections 5 and 26(b); People v. Tumulak, G.R. No. 206054, July 25, 2016: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/62182
records.Controlling Doctrine: An overt, interrupted offer to sell dangerous drugs is an attempted sale punished as the consummated offense under Section 26(b).

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Private Conspirator After Public Officer’s Death
records.Essay Question: The Ombudsman found probable cause against Governor Rocky and Quentin, a private individual, who both allegedly conspired in committing a violation of Section 3(e) of Republic Act No. 3019 or the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act. However, Governor Rocky was killed in an ambush. Yet, the Ombudsman still filed the information against Quentin before the Sandiganbayan. Quentin moved to quash the information on the ground of extinction of criminal liability. Quentin argued that the prosecution for violation of the anti-graft law cannot prosper with the death of Governor Rocky because there is no public officer charged in the information. Is Quentin’s criminal liability extinguished with the death of Governor Rocky? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Governor Rocky’s death did not extinguish Quentin’s own potential criminal liability.

Legal Basis: Article 89 of the Revised Penal Code extinguishes only the deceased accused’s personal criminal liability. A private person may be prosecuted under Republic Act No. 3019 when alleged to have conspired with a public officer. People v. Go holds that the law requires the private person’s conspiracy with a public officer but does not invariably require both to remain jointly indicted when the public officer can no longer be charged because of death.

Application: The information alleges that Quentin conspired with Governor Rocky while the latter was a public officer. Governor Rocky’s death bars prosecution of him personally, but it neither erases the alleged conspiracy nor transfers that personal extinguishment to Quentin.

Conclusion: The prosecution against Quentin may proceed, subject to proof of every element beyond reasonable doubt.

records.Controlling Doctrine: The death of a public officer extinguishes only that officer’s liability; a private alleged conspirator may be prosecuted alone.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Conspiracy and Multiple Counts of Rape
records.Essay Question: Alvin and Dennis together with a John Doe, who remained unidentified and at large, were charged with the crime of rape. The information reads: “Alvin, Dennis, and John Doe, through force, violence, and intimidation, conspiring together and mutually helping one another, did then and there, willfully, unlawfully and feloniously have carnal knowledge of AAA and took turns raping her, by inserting their penises into the vagina of AAA, to her damage and prejudice.” At the trial, the prosecution established that the rapes were committed in the following order, first by Alvin, second by Dennis, third by John Doe, and fourth by Alvin again. The trial court convicted Alvin and Dennis of three counts of rape to the exclusion of the rape that John Doe committed. Is the judgment of conviction correct as to the number of rapes? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Alvin and Dennis are each liable for four counts of rape if the charged conspiracy was proved.

Legal Basis: In conspiracy, the act of one conspirator in furtherance of the common design is the act of all. People v. Diega holds that a rapist is responsible not only for the rape personally committed but also for the rapes committed by co-conspirators, even when a co-conspirator is unidentified or at large.

Application: The four penetrations were separately consummated pursuant to the alleged joint design. Alvin and Dennis are therefore answerable for John Doe’s rape as well as the rapes each participant personally committed.

Conclusion: The proper number is four counts of rape for each proved conspirator.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Robbery With Homicide Versus Homicide and Theft
records.Essay Question: Levi engaged the escort services of Leo for PHP 50,000.00. Levi and Leo then checked in at the hotel and had sex. Afterwards, Levi paid Leo PHP 10,000.00. Leo felt shortchanged when he received an amount smaller than what was promised. At that instance, Leo grabbed a knife from the kitchen and repeatedly stabbed Levi. Thereafter, Leo rummaged through the belongings of Levi and took his wallet, cellphone, and watch. Leo was charged with and convicted of the special complex crime of robbery with homicide. The trial court explained that the killing was by reason of or on occasion of robbery. Is the judgment of conviction correct as to the crime committed? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Leo is liable for separate crimes of homicide and theft on the stated facts.

Legal Basis: Robbery with homicide requires that the original criminal design be robbery and that the homicide occur by reason of or on occasion of that robbery. Catacutan v. People holds that when the intent to rob arises only after the killing, the taking is an afterthought and the acts constitute separate crimes.

Application: Leo stabbed Levi out of anger over the underpayment. Nothing indicates an intent to steal before or during the attack. Only after the killing did he search the victim’s belongings and take property.

Conclusion: Because robbery was an afterthought, the proper offenses are homicide and theft, not robbery with homicide.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Kidnapping for Ransom With Homicide
records.Essay Question: Domeng, in conspiracy with Dado and Dario, kidnapped and detained 9-year-old Rosanna. They demanded ₱2 million as ransom money from the family of Rosanna in exchange for her life and liberty, which the family agreed to pay. However, Domeng, Dado, and Dario killed Rosanna while she was in captivity. What crime, if any, did Domeng, Dado, and Dario commit? Discuss your answer.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Domeng, Dado, and Dario committed kidnapping for ransom with homicide.

Legal Basis: Article 267 of the Revised Penal Code, as amended, treats the killing of a kidnapped victim during detention as part of the special complex crime. People v. Bernardo explains that the classification applies whether the killing was originally intended or arose only during the detention.

Application: The conspirators deprived nine-year-old Rosanna of liberty to extort PHP 2 million from her family, then killed her while she remained captive. The ransom purpose and the death during detention are both present.

Conclusion: They are liable for the special complex crime of kidnapping for ransom with homicide.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Principal by Inducement and Irresistible Force
records.Essay Question: Mark was charged with Rape as a principal by direct participation while his employer, Ado, was charged as a principal by inducement for forcing Mark to commit rape by holding him at gunpoint. Mark was acquitted by the trial court for having acted under the compulsion of an irresistible force. Meanwhile, Ado was convicted of Rape. Ado appealed on the ground that he cannot be held liable because there can be no crime if there is no principal by direct participation. Is the argument of Ado tenable? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Ado’s argument is not tenable.

Legal Basis: Under Articles 12(5) and 17(2) of the Revised Penal Code, one who directly forces another to commit a crime is a principal by inducement, while irresistible force is a personal exempting circumstance of the person compelled. People v. Pantoja explains that a person acting under an exempting circumstance commits the act but is not punishable because intelligence or free will is absent.

Application: Ado used a gun to compel Mark to perform the rape. Mark’s exemption concerns his own lack of free will; it does not erase the criminal act or transfer the exemption to Ado, whose coercion caused the act.

Conclusion: Mark’s acquittal does not relieve Ado, who remains liable as a principal by inducement.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Penal Code, Articles 12(5) and 17(2); People v. Pantoja, G.R. No. 223114, November 29, 2017: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/63595
records.Controlling Doctrine: An exempting circumstance is personal to the compelled actor and does not extinguish the separate liability of the person who directly forced the criminal act.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Reclusion Perpetua and the Three-Fold Rule
records.Essay Question: Miguel was charged with Murder for the death of his neighbor, Nikkolas. During trial, the prosecution established that treachery and evident premeditation attended the killing of Nikkolas. Hence, the trial court found Miguel guilty as charged and sentenced him to suffer the penalty of reclusion perpetua. Upon the lapse of his 30th year in prison, Miguel filed a petition for a writ of habeas corpus on the ground that under the three-fold rule, he had served the maximum of his sentence and that his continued imprisonment is a violation of his right to liberty. Will the petition of Miguel prosper? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Miguel’s habeas corpus petition will not prosper.

Legal Basis: Article 70 of the Revised Penal Code governs the successive service of multiple penalties. Miguel v. Director of the Bureau of Prisons holds that the 30-year computation assigned to a perpetual penalty for Article 70 purposes does not cap reclusion perpetua at 30 years or create an automatic right to release.

Application: Miguel is serving one indivisible penalty, not multiple penalties requiring successive service. His reliance on the three-fold rule is therefore misplaced, and the lapse of 30 years alone does not make his continued detention illegal.

Conclusion: The petition should be denied.

records.Controlling Doctrine: The 30-year computation for a perpetual penalty under the three-fold rule is not an automatic cap on reclusion perpetua and does not authorize release where only one sentence is being served.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Malversation and Accountable Officers
records.Essay Question: Metropolitan Waterworks Sewerage System (MWSS) employee Japar was often assigned to do field work. Every time he does field work, he accomplishes a disbursement voucher for the amount that he needs and liquidates the voucher by submitting receipts to the MWSS cashier, Filomena, at the end of the day. One day, another MWSS employee, Jonas, desperately needed ₱230,000. Taking the same disbursement voucher that Japar habitually signs in the morning, Jonas filled it out with the amount that he needed. He then forged the signature of Japar before presenting it to Filomena, who in turn released the stated amount. After some time, Filomena noticed that the voucher remained unliquidated. When Filomena showed the voucher to Japar, the latter swiftly returned it, telling Filomena that the signature appearing in the voucher was not his. Filomena then realized that Jonas was the one who presented the voucher and took the money. When confronted, Jonas readily admitted to the act. He was eventually convicted of Malversation. Was the conviction of Jonas proper? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Jonas’s conviction for malversation was improper.

Legal Basis: Article 217 of the Revised Penal Code requires that the public officer have custody or control of the public funds by reason of office and be accountable for them. Sarion v. People and Fajardo v. People treat official accountability as an indispensable element; employment in government alone is insufficient.

Application: Jonas obtained the PHP 230,000 only by forging Japar’s voucher. The facts do not show that Jonas was authorized by his office to receive, keep, or account for those funds. His conduct may support another offense, including the panel’s formulation of estafa through falsification of a public document, but it does not satisfy malversation’s accountability element.

Conclusion: The malversation conviction was not proper.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Penal Code, Article 217; Sarion v. People, G.R. Nos. 243029-30, March 18, 2021: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/67371/; Fajardo v. People, G.R. No. 239823, September 25, 2019: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/65695
records.Controlling Doctrine: A public employee cannot be convicted of malversation unless the funds were under that employee’s official custody or control and the employee was accountable for them.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Sarion v. People; Fajardo v. People

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Theft of Lost Property and Finder in Law
records.Essay Question: Before Milet drove to the public market one Sunday, she organized her money by bundling together her dollars worth US$4,000 and placed ₱20,000 in an envelope. She drove to the market, bought shrimps and oysters, then hurried back home to prepare lunch. While she was unloading the food from her car, the bundled US$4,000 unknowingly fell from her bag and rolled over to the sidewalk. At that moment, a lato-lato, owned by 13-year-old Henri, suddenly flew near the car of Milet. When Henri retrieved his lato-lato, he saw the bundled money and secretly picked it up. On his way home, Henri bumped into their gardener, Junie, who saw him carrying the bundled money and grabbed it from him. After hearing where Henri got the money from, Junie took US$2,000 as his balato. Junie immediately exchanged the money to Philippine currency and bought an Omega x Swatch MoonSwatch, a Gucci belt, and the latest Samsung phone. Junie was later arrested and charged with Theft. Junie argued that he could not be liable since he was not the one who found the money. Is Junie correct? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Junie is liable for theft.

Legal Basis: Article 308 of the Revised Penal Code covers the appropriation of lost property instead of returning it to the owner or local authorities. Pante v. People holds that liability is not confined to the first physical finder; a person who knowingly receives and appropriates lost property may be a “finder in law.”

Application: Junie knew from Henri that the US dollars belonged to someone else. Rather than return the money, he took half, converted it, and spent it for personal benefit, demonstrating intent to gain.

Conclusion: Junie’s claim that he was not the original finder does not defeat his liability for theft.

records.Controlling Doctrine: A person who knowingly receives and appropriates lost property can be a finder in law and liable for theft even if another person physically found the property first.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Self-Defense and Performance of Duty
records.Essay Question:
Police officer John ran after Randy who had just killed Willy in John’s presence. John fired at Randy in an attempt to stop him in his tracks. In response, Randy fired back at John, hitting him. John was seriously wounded but survived due to timely medical assistance. Randy was then charged with Frustrated Homicide. During the trial, Randy claimed self-defense.

Is Randy’s claim of self-defense tenable? Explain briefly. (5 points)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Randy’s claim of self-defense is not tenable.

Legal Basis: Article 11(1) of the Revised Penal Code makes unlawful aggression an indispensable element of self-defense. Galang v. Court of Appeals explains that without unlawful aggression, there can be no complete or incomplete self-defense. A police officer’s necessary act to arrest or stop a person who has just committed a killing is an act in the performance of duty, not unlawful aggression.

Application: John personally witnessed Randy kill Willy, pursued him, and fired to stop his escape. On the stated facts, John’s conduct was connected with the lawful performance of police duty. Randy’s return fire therefore did not repel unlawful aggression.

Conclusion: Because the indispensable element of unlawful aggression is absent, Randy cannot successfully invoke self-defense.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Penal Code, Article 11(1); Galang v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 128536, January 31, 2000: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/51007
records.Controlling Doctrine: Self-defense fails when the supposed aggression is a police officer’s lawful performance of duty, because unlawful aggression is indispensable.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Treachery and Multiple Murder
records.Essay Question:
Moe, Curly, and Larry were drinking and singing inside a karaoke bar when suddenly, Buboy entered the bar and without warning, immediately shot all three of them using a caliber .45 pistol. Thereafter, Buboy ran out of the bar to escape. Moe, Curly, and Larry died instantly due to gunshot wounds in their heads and bodies. With the help of eyewitnesses, Buboy was arrested. After inquest, the prosecutor charged Buboy with three counts of Homicide.

Do you agree with the charge of Homicide against Buboy? Explain briefly. (5 points)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. On the stated facts, Buboy should be charged with three counts of murder qualified by treachery.

Legal Basis: Article 248 of the Revised Penal Code classifies a killing attended by treachery as murder. People v. Agsalog explains that treachery exists when the means of attack gives the victim no opportunity to defend or retaliate and is consciously adopted to ensure execution without risk to the attacker.

Application: Buboy entered without warning and immediately shot the three victims while they were drinking and singing. The sudden gun attack left them defenseless, and each death is a distinct killing.

Conclusion: The proper charges are three counts of murder, not homicide.

records.Controlling Doctrine: A sudden, consciously adopted attack that leaves victims no opportunity to defend themselves constitutes treachery and qualifies each killing as murder.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Accident, Unlawful Arrest, and Article 4
records.Essay Question:
Michael was driving along the highway when he executed a prohibited U-Turn. Dyords, a police officer, accosted Michael for the traffic violation. A verbal argument ensued between them. Dyords suddenly drew his service firearm, and pointed it at Michael. Dyords ordered Michael to alight from his car, which the latter obeyed. Dyords then handcuffed Michael and pinned his head and body against the pavement until he could no longer breathe. Michael died. Charged with Homicide, Dyords interposed the exempting circumstance of accident as a defense.

If you were the judge, how would you resolve Dyords’ defense? Explain briefly. (5 points)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: I would reject Dyords’s defense of accident.

Legal Basis: Article 12(4) of the Revised Penal Code requires a person invoking accident to have been performing a lawful act with due care. Article 4 makes a person criminally liable for the natural consequences of a felony. People v. Cristobal, applying Luz v. People, explains that a traffic violation ordinarily calls for confiscation of the driver’s license rather than a custodial arrest.

Application: Dyords did not merely enforce the traffic rule. He drew a firearm, handcuffed Michael, and pinned him to the pavement until he suffocated. Those acts were neither a lawful, careful performance of duty nor a mere accident. The fatal consequence flowed from Dyords’s unlawful restraint and force.

Conclusion: The accident exemption does not apply, and Dyords remains criminally liable for the resulting homicide.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Penal Code, Articles 4 and 12(4); People v. Cristobal, G.R. No. 234207, June 10, 2019: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/65317; Picardal v. People, G.R. No. 235749, June 19, 2019: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/65319
records.Controlling Doctrine: Accident is unavailable when the accused was not performing a lawful act with due care; a fatal consequence naturally flowing from unlawful restraint remains attributable under Article 4.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Spontaneous Desistance in Attempted Parricide
records.Essay Question:
A police officer responded to a disturbance call at around 1:30 p.m. in an apartment in Quezon City. Upon his arrival, the police officer encountered Sisa stabbing her 1-year old child with a kitchen knife. The police officer grabbed Sisa and the latter threw the knife on the floor. Sisa was immediately taken into custody. Despite suffering multiple stab wounds on her back, the child survived. During the trial, Sisa insisted that she can only be held liable for Attempted Parricide because she voluntarily desisted when she threw down the knife.

Is Sisa’s contention tenable? Explain briefly. (5 points)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Sisa’s reliance on voluntary desistance is not tenable.

Legal Basis: Article 6 of the Revised Penal Code recognizes spontaneous desistance only when the offender stops by a free and spontaneous act before performing all acts of execution. People v. Lizada explains that desistance prompted by an external constraint is not spontaneous and does not erase liability for an attempted felony.

Application: Sisa dropped the knife only after the police officer physically grabbed her. Her cessation was caused by an external intervention, not by an unprompted decision to abandon the attack.

Conclusion: Sisa cannot invoke spontaneous desistance to avoid liability; the proper stage of parricide must be determined from the acts of execution and injuries proved.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Penal Code, Articles 6 and 246; People v. Lizada, G.R. Nos. 143468-71, January 24, 2003: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/44312
records.Controlling Doctrine: Desistance caused by police intervention is not spontaneous and does not exempt an offender from liability for the attempted felony already begun.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Robbery With Homicide and Integrated Offenses
records.Essay Question:
Anna and Barbara, while working inside their sari-sari store, saw Javier and Jorge robbing an elderly woman of her purse and brutally beating her to death. Anna and Barbara immediately ran outside and, when they tried to help the elderly woman, Javier and Jorge stabbed both of them. Thereafter, Javier and Jorge ran away with the elderly woman’s purse. Anna suffered one stab wound which punctured her lung, but she survived due to timely medical assistance. Barbara, however, died as a result of nine stab wounds, one of which pierced through her spleen.

If you were the prosecutor, what crime/s will you file against Javier and Jorge for: (i) the death of the elderly woman, (ii) the death of Barbara, and (iii) the injuries sustained by Anna? Explain briefly. (5 points)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Javier and Jorge should be charged with one special complex crime of robbery with homicide.

Legal Basis: Article 294(1) of the Revised Penal Code treats homicide committed by reason of or on occasion of robbery as a special complex crime. People v. Daguman holds that all homicides and physical injuries committed on the occasion of the robbery are integrated into the single, indivisible offense, regardless of the number or identity of the victims.

Application: The elderly woman was killed during the taking of her purse. Barbara was killed and Anna was wounded when they intervened while the robbers were completing and escaping from the robbery. Those violent acts occurred on the occasion of the same robbery.

Conclusion: The two deaths and Anna’s injuries are absorbed in one charge of robbery with homicide.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Impossible Crime of Theft
records.Essay Question:
Jenny obtained a fire insurance from YG Insurance Co. (YG). In payment of the policy, she issued a postdated check payable to cash in the amount of Php 15,000.00 which was handed to Lisa, YG’s sales agent. Lisa did not remit the check to YG. Instead, Lisa deposited it in her husband’s bank account, but the check was dishonored for having been drawn from a closed account.

What crime, if any, was committed by Lisa and, if there was any, what is its prescribed penalty? Explain briefly. (5 points)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Lisa committed an impossible crime of theft.

Legal Basis: Article 4(2) of the Revised Penal Code punishes an act that would be an offense against persons or property were its accomplishment not inherently impossible or the means inadequate or ineffectual. Jacinto v. People applies this rule when an accused appropriates a check that turns out to have no value. Article 59 prescribes arresto mayor or prisión correccional, depending on the social danger and degree of criminality shown.

Application: Lisa, with intent to gain, appropriated YG’s check by depositing it into her husband’s account instead of remitting it. Theft could not be consummated because the closed-account check had no realizable value, a fact unknown to her.

Conclusion: Lisa is liable for an impossible crime of theft, punishable within Article 59’s stated range as judicially determined.

records.Controlling Doctrine: Appropriating a check with intent to gain may constitute an impossible crime of theft when the check is valueless for a reason unknown to the offender.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Single Quasi-Offense of Reckless Imprudence
records.Essay Question:
On May 15, 2013 at around 3:00 a.m., Lucy, Mary, and Raphael were on board a passenger jeepney, with Raphael behind the wheel. They were traversing the highway on the southbound lane.

Meanwhile, a Virgen Bus, driven by Kiko, was traveling along the northbound lane. Kiko overtook the vehicle in front of him, which caused him to occupy the opposite lane where the jeepney was on. With the Virgen Bus traveling at a high speed, Raphael tried to avoid the collision but failed. The bus hit the jeepney which resulted in Raphael’s death, serious physical injuries to Lucy and Mary, and extensive damage to the jeepney amounting to Php 500,000.00.

The public prosecutor filed two Informations charging Kiko for two separate offenses: (i) Reckless Imprudence resulting in Serious Physical Injuries for the injuries suffered by the passengers; and (ii) Reckless Imprudence resulting in Homicide and Damage to Property for Raphael’s death and the damage to the jeepney.

Is the public prosecutor correct? Explain briefly. (5 points)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The prosecutor should file one information covering the single quasi-offense and all its consequences.

Legal Basis: Article 365 of the Revised Penal Code punishes the negligent act itself, not each resulting injury as a separate intentional felony. Ivler v. Modesto-San Pedro holds that a single negligent act producing death, physical injuries, and property damage constitutes one quasi-offense of reckless imprudence.

Application: Kiko’s single act of recklessly overtaking caused one collision and all the resulting death, injuries, and property damage. Splitting those consequences into two informations treats the effects as separate offenses despite their single negligent source.

Conclusion: One information should charge reckless imprudence resulting in homicide, serious physical injuries, and damage to property.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Penal Code, Article 365; Ivler v. Modesto-San Pedro, G.R. No. 172716, November 17, 2010: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/34407
records.Controlling Doctrine: A single negligent act is one quasi-offense of reckless imprudence even when it produces death, bodily injuries, and property damage.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Drug Paraphernalia and Forensic Examination
records.Essay Question:
Sometime in 2011, while police officers were conducting a foot patrol in connection with the report of rampant illegal activities in the area, police officer Pepe saw Raul inside a small shanty holding a disposable syringe. Being a police officer for almost 15 years and having previously made more than ten arrests involving possession of drug paraphernalia, Pepe entered through the open door of Raul’s shanty and arrested him. Inside the shanty, 23 more pieces of disposable syringes and empty ampules were seized from Raul. Pepe immediately marked the seized items, took photographs thereof, and conducted an inventory in the presence of Raul, a barangay kagawad, a representative from the Department of Justice (DOJ), and a media practitioner. The seized items were turned over to the evidence custodian, who kept them in a sealed container in the police station.

During the trial of Raul for the crime of Illegal Possession of Drug Paraphernalia, police officer Pepe, the sole witness for the prosecution, testified as narrated above. After which, the prosecution rested its case. The defense did not present any evidence.

If you were the judge, would you convict or acquit Raul for the crime charged? Explain briefly. (5 points)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Raul should be acquitted because the prosecution did not prove beyond reasonable doubt that the ordinary items were drug paraphernalia.

Legal Basis: Sections 12 and 21 of Republic Act No. 9165 require proof that the seized equipment was fit or intended for introducing dangerous drugs into the body and require submission to the PDEA forensic laboratory. Cuico v. People holds that ordinary items such as syringes cannot be treated as drug paraphernalia from appearance or police opinion alone; forensic testing is material to identity and chain of custody.

Application: The prosecution produced syringes and empty ampoules but no laboratory result showing traces of a dangerous drug or their prohibited intended use. Pepe’s experience and sole testimony cannot cure that evidentiary gap.

Conclusion: Reasonable doubt remains as to an essential element, so Raul must be acquitted.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Republic Act No. 9165, Sections 12 and 21; Cuico v. People, G.R. No. 232293, December 9, 2020: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/67047
records.Controlling Doctrine: Ordinary syringes and ampoules cannot support a drug-paraphernalia conviction without proof, including required forensic examination, of their prohibited drug-related character.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Child Abuse and Intent to Debase
records.Essay Question:
Joben, a school principal, called high school students Paula and Gina, both 15 years old, to the faculty room regarding the sexual text message circulating around campus which made reference to Joben’s daughter. In front of teachers and some students, Joben shouted at Paula and Gina, asking them who sent the said text message. Joben also threatened to sue them and said: “Siguro nainggit kayo sa anak ko kasi maganda sya, matalino at mayaman. Sabihin nyo kasi sa mga magulang nyo magsumikap sila para maging mayaman din kayo. Di yung tatamad-tamad.” Joben then raised her middle finger in front of Paula and Gina, saying “Mga burikat (whore)!”

Later that day, Paula and Gina narrated the incident to their parents and said that they were ashamed of going back to school.

Is Joben guilty of violating Section 10(a) of Republic Act No. 7610 for other acts of child abuse? Explain briefly. (5 points)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No, on the stated facts and controlling case analogy, the required intent to debase, degrade, or demean was not proved beyond reasonable doubt.

Legal Basis: Section 10(a) of Republic Act No. 7610 punishes other acts of child abuse. Brinas v. People holds that, where the alleged act is inherently non-abusive in the statutory sense, the prosecution must establish the specific intent to debase, degrade, or demean the child’s intrinsic worth and dignity.

Application: Joben’s words and gesture were offensive and humiliating, but the episode arose in the heat of anger over a message involving her daughter. Those circumstances do not, without more, prove the specific statutory intent beyond reasonable doubt.

Conclusion: Joben should be acquitted of the Section 10(a) charge, without implying that her conduct was proper or free from other consequences.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Republic Act No. 7610, Section 10(a); Brinas v. People, G.R. No. 254005, June 23, 2021: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/67545
records.Controlling Doctrine: Offensive words to minors do not automatically constitute Section 10(a) child abuse; the required statutory intent must be proved beyond reasonable doubt.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Procurement Violations and Section 3(e)
records.Essay Question:
In 2003, the Province of Davao del Sur purchased two vehicles for the use of the Governor and Vice Governor, respectively. The purchase requests, which were all signed by Luis as then Governor of the province, requested for the acquisition of one unit of Ford Ranger XLT 4x4 and one unit of Toyota Hilux 4x4. The procurement of the subject vehicles did not undergo competitive public bidding as it was effected through direct purchase. The mode of procurement was approved by the members of the Bids and Awards Committee (BAC) of the province. The two vehicles were delivered to the provincial government, and after inspection and acceptance by the concerned officials, payments were issued to the suppliers.

Subsequently, a complaint was filed by a concerned citizen before the Office of the Ombudsman-Mindanao (OMB) claiming that the purchase of the provincial government violated the procurement law. The OMB, after due investigation, verified that the provincial government did not comply with the required procedure of the procurement law. Based on this finding, the OMB filed with the Sandiganbayan an Information against Luis and the members of the BAC for violation of Section 3(e) of Republic Act No. 3019.

The Sandiganbayan found Luis and the members of the BAC guilty on the sole reason that violation of the procurement law constitutes evident bad faith and manifest partiality on the part of the accused.

Is the Sandiganbayan correct? Explain briefly. (5 points)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. A procurement-law violation alone does not establish every element of Section 3(e) of Republic Act No. 3019.

Legal Basis: Section 3(e) requires, among other elements, manifest partiality, evident bad faith, or gross inexcusable negligence, plus undue injury to a party or an unwarranted benefit, advantage, or preference. Martel v. People holds that breach of procurement rules does not automatically prove those separate statutory elements.

Application: The conviction rested solely on the absence of competitive bidding. The facts, as stated, do not independently identify the required culpable mode or show undue injury or an unwarranted private benefit.

Conclusion: The Sandiganbayan’s reasoning was insufficient, and conviction under Section 3(e) cannot rest on the procurement irregularity alone.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Republic Act No. 3019, Section 3(e); Martel v. People, G.R. Nos. 224720-23 and 224765-68, February 2, 2021: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/67194
records.Controlling Doctrine: A procurement-law violation is not automatically a Section 3(e) graft offense; the prosecution must separately prove culpable conduct and undue injury or unwarranted benefit.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Robbery by Intimidation and Abuse of Public Position
records.Essay Question:
One Sunday afternoon, while standing at the corner of C.P. Garcia and Katipunan Avenues, an off-duty police officer accosted a motorcycle rider and asked them to alight. The off-duty police officer then inspected the motorcycle's compartment box.

Pretending that a sachet of shabu was found, the off-duty police officer demanded PHP1,000.00 in order to prevent an arrest.

Fearful of being incarcerated for life for a crime that was not really committed, the motorcycle rider readily complied. Unknown to the off-duty police officer, a surveillance camera caught the entire incident.

Will a charge of robbery prosper against the off-duty police officer? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. The officer committed robbery by intimidation.

Legal Basis: Articles 293 and 294(5) of the Revised Penal Code require an unlawful taking of another’s personal property, with intent to gain, by violence or intimidation. Sosas v. People holds that law-enforcement officers who abuse their authority to intimidate a person into paying money commit robbery by extortion.

Application: The officer falsely claimed to have found shabu and used the threat of arrest and severe punishment to compel payment. The rider’s apparent consent was produced by fear, while intent to gain is shown by the officer’s demand and receipt of the money. His police position supplied the intimidation even though he was off duty.

Conclusion: A charge of robbery by intimidation will prosper, with abuse of public position considered when legally proper.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Penal Code, Articles 14(1), 293, and 294(5); Sosas v. People, G.R. Nos. 249283 and 249400, April 26, 2023: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/69076
records.Controlling Doctrine: A police officer who exploits apparent authority and threatens arrest to obtain money commits robbery by intimidation.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Child Cruelty and Excessive Discipline
records.Essay Question:
To motivate their eight-year-old daughter to study well and have a better future, her parents resorted to making her kneel on rice spread on the floor, spanking her with a bamboo stick, or requiring her to stand in the rain for hours if her grades fell below 80 in any subject.

Did the parents commit a crime? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. The parents’ excessive punishments constitute child cruelty punishable under Section 10(a) of Republic Act No. 7610.

Legal Basis: Section 10(a) of Republic Act No. 7610 punishes other acts of child abuse. Fernandez v. People recognizes that parental discipline is excluded from cruelty only when it is reasonable in manner and moderate in degree and does not cause physical or psychological injury.

Application: Prolonged standing in the rain, kneeling on rice, and striking an eight-year-old with a bamboo stick are disproportionate to the educational purpose asserted. The repeated methods inflict degrading physical and psychological punishment beyond reasonable parental correction.

Conclusion: The parents may be held liable for child cruelty under Section 10(a), subject to proof of the statutory elements beyond reasonable doubt.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Republic Act No. 7610, Section 10(a); Fernandez v. People, G.R. No. 217542, November 21, 2018: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/64751
records.Controlling Doctrine: Parental discipline loses statutory protection when its manner is unreasonable, excessive, and injurious or degrading to the child.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Economic Abuse Through Denial of Support
records.Essay Question:
An estranged married couple decided to separate. As part of their amicable settlement, they agreed to ask their 14-year-old child to choose a parent with whom to live.

The child chose the mother.

Displeased, the husband ceased providing for the child's tuition and the wife's support. The husband was a vice president of a highly profitable company.

Did the husband commit any crime? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes, if the deliberate deprivation was used to control or punish the wife or child as the facts indicate, the husband committed economic abuse under Republic Act No. 9262.

Legal Basis: Section 5(e)(2) of Republic Act No. 9262 penalizes deprivation or denial of financial support legally due to a woman or her child when committed in the statutory context. Melgar v. People confirms that deliberate denial of support to a child may constitute violence against women and children, while Acharon v. People requires proof of the legally due support and the prohibited purpose or effect.

Application: The husband had financial capacity but stopped support immediately because the child chose the mother. The timing and stated displeasure show that support was withheld to pressure or retaliate against the wife and child.

Conclusion: The facts support prosecution for economic abuse, subject to proof of every element beyond reasonable doubt.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Republic Act No. 9262, Section 5(e)(2); Melgar v. People, G.R. No. 223477, February 14, 2018: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/63887; Acharon v. People, G.R. No. 224946, November 9, 2021: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68085
records.Controlling Doctrine: Deliberately withholding legally due support to control or punish a woman or her child may constitute economic abuse under Republic Act No. 9262.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Unauthorized Disclosure of Personal Information
records.Essay Question:
The head of a big company's human resources division copied and shared an employee's physical and email address, birthdate, civil status, and some photos with a friend who found the employee attractive.

Did the head of the human resources division commit a crime? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. The unauthorized sharing may constitute unauthorized disclosure under the Data Privacy Act of 2012.

Legal Basis: Republic Act No. 10173 protects personal and sensitive personal information and limits processing and disclosure to lawful grounds. Section 32 penalizes a personal information controller or processor, or its responsible officers, employees, or agents, who discloses personal information to a third party without consent. Zoleta v. Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas explains that sensitive and privileged information receive a special regime of protection under Philippine privacy law.

Application: The human-resources head obtained the data through the employment relationship and disclosed it for a friend’s private interest, without the employee’s consent or any stated lawful basis.

Conclusion: The facts support liability for unauthorized disclosure, subject to proof of the accused’s covered role and the other statutory elements.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Republic Act No. 10173, Sections 3, 12, 13, and 32; Zoleta v. Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, G.R. No. 258888, August 29, 2023: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/69447
records.Controlling Doctrine: Employment access to personal data does not authorize disclosure to a third party for a private purpose without consent or another lawful basis.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Gender-Based Street Sexual Harassment
records.Essay Question:
While a person was passing through a construction site for a new Hall of Justice building, construction workers shouted: “Hoy bakla, halika rito at haplusin mo ‘ko!” “Hoy bakla, ang pangit mo!” “Bakla, mukha ka pa ring lalaki kahit ano'ng gawin mo!”

The person victimized by these remarks asks you: Was a crime committed by the workers who shouted these statements? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. The statements constitute gender-based sexual harassment in a public space under the Safe Spaces Act.

Legal Basis: Sections 4 and 11 of Republic Act No. 11313 cover unwanted sexual remarks and transphobic, homophobic, or sexist slurs made in streets and other public spaces. Falcis v. Civil Registrar General recognizes that the Safe Spaces Act specifically addresses and penalizes transphobic, homophobic, and sexist slurs.

Application: The workers directed unwanted sexual invitations and repeated homophobic ridicule at a passerby because of perceived sex, gender, sexual orientation, identity, or expression. A construction site along a passage open to the public falls within the law’s public-space protection.

Conclusion: The workers may be prosecuted for gender-based street and public-spaces sexual harassment.

records.Controlling Doctrine: Homophobic or transphobic slurs and unwanted sexual invitations directed at a person in a public space are punishable under the Safe Spaces Act.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Unpunishable Proposal to Commit Murder
records.Essay Question:
During one of their intense operational meetings, the campaign manager of a presidential candidate openly suggested, “Dapat ipapatay na lang natin ang mga bumabatikos sa kandidato natin.”

Later, the campaign manager was charged with the crime of Proposal to Commit Murder.

Can the campaign manager be convicted of the offense charged? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Proposal to commit murder is not independently punishable under the Revised Penal Code.

Legal Basis: Article 8 of the Revised Penal Code provides that conspiracy and proposal to commit a felony are punishable only when the law specifically prescribes a penalty. Pascual v. People reiterates this limiting rule. The Code specifically punishes proposals for certain offenses, but it does not create an offense of proposal to commit murder.

Application: Even assuming that the statement was a proposal rather than rhetoric or a mere suggestion, no penal provision specifically punishes proposal to commit murder. Penal statutes cannot be extended by analogy.

Conclusion: The campaign manager cannot be convicted of the offense charged.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Penal Code, Article 8; Pascual v. People, G.R. Nos. 241248 and 241257-59, June 16, 2021: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/67750
records.Controlling Doctrine: Proposal to commit a felony is punishable only when a statute specifically provides a penalty; proposal to commit murder is not such an offense.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Theft Through Temporary Taking and Use
records.Essay Question:
During a Senate hearing in aid of legislation, a Senator's staff member took a resource person's mobile phone without their consent or knowledge.

While the hearing was ongoing, the staff member read the resource person's messages contained in the mobile phone and hurriedly wrote notes which were passed to the Senator.

Thereafter, the staff surreptitiously returned the mobile phone.

The resource person would not have noticed that the mobile phone was taken had it not been for a TikTok video posted by a journalist who was present during the hearing. The TikTok video caught the entire act of the Senator's staff member. The TikTok video even had accompanying music and narration.

The video became viral.

Can the staff member be liable for Theft of the mobile phone? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. The temporary taking and unauthorized use can constitute consummated theft.

Legal Basis: Article 308 of the Revised Penal Code requires taking another’s personal property, without consent, with intent to gain, and without violence, intimidation, or force. People v. Bustinera holds that the mere unauthorized use of property unlawfully taken constitutes gain, and Valenzuela v. People holds that theft is consummated upon completed taking with intent to gain.

Application: The staff member secretly obtained control of the phone, used its contents for the hearing, and acted without the owner’s knowledge or consent. Returning the device after obtaining that unauthorized benefit does not undo the completed taking.

Conclusion: The staff member may be held liable for consummated theft.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Penal Code, Article 308; People v. Bustinera, G.R. No. 148233, June 8, 2004: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/46991; Valenzuela v. People, G.R. No. 160188, June 21, 2007: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/41676
records.Controlling Doctrine: Unauthorized temporary use supplies intent to gain, and later return does not erase a theft already consummated by completed taking.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Accessory by Concealing the Body of the Crime
records.Essay Question:
In an act of rage while playing golf, a high-ranking public official hit a caddy with a golf club at hole number 9 of a golf course. The caddy fell and died immediately.

The public official called a loyal security guard who did not witness the incident. The security guard was instructed to put the caddy's lifeless body in the golf cart and dump it in the nearby lake. The public official wanted to make it appear that the caddy died of drowning.

The corpus delicti of the crime was discovered. Both the high-ranking public official and the security guard were charged as co-conspirators for the crime of Homicide.

Can the security guard be convicted as a principal to the crime of Homicide? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The security guard is not a principal in the homicide but may be liable as an accessory.

Legal Basis: Articles 17 and 19 of the Revised Penal Code distinguish principals from accessories. An accessory, with knowledge of the crime and without prior participation as principal or accomplice, acts afterward by concealing or destroying the body of the crime to prevent discovery. People v. Lamsen applies Article 19(2) to post-crime concealment.

Application: The guard neither participated in nor agreed to the killing before it occurred. His conduct began only after the caddy was dead, when he concealed and dumped the body to mislead investigators.

Conclusion: He cannot be convicted as a principal or co-conspirator in homicide on these facts, but he may be convicted as an accessory under Article 19(2).

records.Controlling Doctrine: A person who joins only after a killing and conceals the corpse to prevent discovery is an accessory, not a principal in the homicide.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Indeterminate Sentence Law Exception
records.Essay Question:
A crime defined in the Revised Penal Code is punishable by arresto menor.

Finding the accused guilty beyond reasonable doubt of the crime, should the judge apply the Indeterminate Sentence Law? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The Indeterminate Sentence Law does not apply.

Legal Basis: Section 2 of Act No. 4103 excludes persons whose maximum term of imprisonment does not exceed one year. People v. Hamoy expressly applies that exception. Under Article 27 of the Revised Penal Code, arresto menor runs from one day to 30 days.

Application: The statutory maximum for arresto menor is only 30 days, far below the one-year threshold. The sentence therefore falls within the express statutory exception.

Conclusion: The judge should impose the proper straight penalty and should not fix minimum and maximum indeterminate terms.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Act No. 4103, Section 2; Revised Penal Code, Article 27; People v. Hamoy, G.R. No. 227505, October 2, 2017: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/63708
records.Controlling Doctrine: The Indeterminate Sentence Law does not apply when the maximum imprisonment does not exceed one year, including arresto menor.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Death of Accused Pending Appeal
records.Essay Question:
A prisoner who had been convicted, but whose appeal was pending, died due to complications caused by COVID-19.

Should the prisoner's pending appeal be dismissed as a consequence? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. The criminal case and appeal should be dismissed and terminated because death occurred before final judgment.

Legal Basis: Article 89(1) of the Revised Penal Code extinguishes criminal liability by death. People v. Brillantes, applying People v. Bayotas, holds that an accused’s death pending appeal extinguishes criminal liability and civil liability based solely on the offense, while civil claims based on other sources of obligation may survive in a proper separate action.

Application: Because the conviction was still under appeal, it was not final when the prisoner died. There is no longer an accused upon whom the criminal penalty may be imposed.

Conclusion: The appeal should be dismissed, criminal liability and civil liability ex delicto are extinguished, without prejudice to independently sourced civil claims allowed by law.

records.Controlling Doctrine: Death before final judgment extinguishes criminal liability and civil liability ex delicto, while independently sourced civil claims may survive.

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Illegal Gambling and Poverty Defense
records.Essay Question:
A person arrested for playing cara y cruz was charged with violation of Presidential Decree No. 1602 or the Anti-Gambling Law.

The lawyer for the accused argues that the case should be dismissed based on an exempting circumstance, which is that the accused is poor. The lawyer argues that unlike those who gamble in big casinos with astronomical sums of money, cara y cruz is the accused's only means of entertainment. In addition, the lawyer explains that gamblers from China, where gambling is illegal, are even welcomed in the Philippines.

Is the lawyer's argument legally tenable? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Poverty and the stated comparisons are not exempting circumstances and do not legalize the prohibited gambling act.

Legal Basis: Presidential Decree No. 1602 penalizes unauthorized gambling, while Article 12 of the Revised Penal Code exhaustively identifies exempting circumstances. Yun Kwan Byung v. Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corporation states the general rule that gambling is illegal unless affirmatively authorized by law.

Application: Playing cara y cruz is not made lawful by the accused’s poverty, motive, or comparison with licensed gambling. None of those considerations appears among Article 12’s exemptions, and lawful casino gaming rests on specific statutory authorization.

Conclusion: The defense does not justify dismissal of the illegal-gambling charge.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Presidential Decree No. 1602; Revised Penal Code, Article 12; Yun Kwan Byung v. Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corporation, G.R. No. 163553, December 11, 2009: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/51152
records.Controlling Doctrine: Unauthorized gambling remains punishable despite poverty or benign motive; licensed gambling is different because it rests on affirmative legal authorization.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Yun Kwan Byung v. Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corporation

records.Subject: Criminal Law
records.Topic: Homicide and Praeter Intentionem
records.Essay Question:
While attending to an Enhanced Community Quarantine barangay checkpoint, a barangay tanod confronted a resident for non-essential travel. Infuriated by the barangay tanod's tone, the resident punched the tanod's head. The barangay tanod fell, sustained brain hemorrhage, and died as a result.

Charged with Homicide, the resident denies liability, arguing that there can be no conviction if there is no intent to cause the barangay tanod's death.

Is the resident's defense tenable? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The lack of intent to kill does not relieve the resident of liability for the death, although praeter intentionem may mitigate the penalty if proved.

Legal Basis: Article 4(1) of the Revised Penal Code makes a person committing a felony liable although the wrongful act differs from that intended. Article 13(3) recognizes the mitigating circumstance that the offender did not intend to commit so grave a wrong. Urbano v. People applies liability for the resulting death while appreciating that mitigating circumstance when the means used and surrounding facts show a lesser intended harm.

Application: The intentional punch was a felony, and the tanod’s fatal fall and brain hemorrhage directly followed it. The resident is answerable for that natural consequence even if only physical injury was intended.

Conclusion: The homicide defense fails, but lack of intent to cause so grave a wrong may mitigate liability.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Revised Penal Code, Articles 4(1) and 13(3); Urbano v. People, G.R. No. 182750, January 20, 2009: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/48637
records.Controlling Doctrine: An offender is liable for a death naturally caused by an intentional assault even without intent to kill, though praeter intentionem may mitigate the penalty.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Urbano v. People
