records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Topic: Local Taxation — Injunction
records.Essay Question: The City Treasurer served to Luminous Star Corporation (LSC) a Notice of Assessment (NOA) for basic local business taxes (LBT) in the amount of PHP 900,000.00, exclusive of interest and penalties. LSC filed a protest before the City Treasurer but was denied. LSC appealed to the Metropolitan Trial Court (MeTC) and prayed for a writ of preliminary injunction to prevent the collection of assessed taxes. The City Treasurer opposed the application for injunctive relief and contended that the courts cannot enjoin the collection of taxes. May the MeTC issue an injunctive relief against the City Treasurer from collecting the local taxes? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes, if the requisites for injunction are proved.

Legal Basis: The Local Government Code contains no counterpart to the National Internal Revenue Code’s express anti-injunction rule for national taxes. Angeles City v. Angeles Electric Corporation holds that courts may issue preliminary injunctions in local-tax cases when ordinary equitable requisites are satisfied.

Application: The assessment concerns local business tax. The City Treasurer’s categorical claim of an absolute statutory prohibition is therefore incorrect, although LSC must still establish a clear right, urgency, and irreparable injury.

Conclusion: The MeTC may issue injunction upon proof of the procedural and substantive requisites.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Local Government Code; Rule 58 of the Rules of Court; Angeles City v. Angeles Electric Corporation, G.R. No. 166134, June 29, 2010: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/53986
records.Controlling Doctrine: Collection of local taxes is not subject to the NIRC’s absolute anti-injunction provision; ordinary injunction rules apply.

records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Topic: Tax Refunds — Premature Judicial Claim
records.Essay Question: On August 23, 2024, Topaz Gems Industries (TGI) filed with the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) an administrative claim for refund of overpaid final withholding tax on dividends paid in 2023. On August 28, 2024, TGI filed a judicial claim for refund before the Court of Tax Appeals (CTA). The BIR opposed the judicial claim for refund and contended that the CTA lacks jurisdiction over the case. The BIR added that the judicial claim was premature having been filed without prior resolution of the administrative claim. Does the CTA have jurisdiction over the judicial claim for refund? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The judicial claim was prematurely filed under the Ease of Paying Taxes Act rules already effective in August 2024.

Legal Basis: Section 229 of the NIRC, as amended by Republic Act No. 11976, gives the Commissioner of Internal Revenue 180 days to act on a refund claim; appeal lies within 30 days after denial or expiration of that period. Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Carrier Air Conditioning Philippines, Inc. treats compliance with statutory refund waiting periods as jurisdictional.

Application: TGI went to the CTA only five days after its administrative filing, before denial and before expiration of 180 days.

Conclusion: The CTA lacks jurisdiction over the premature judicial claim.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: NIRC, Section 229, as amended by Republic Act No. 11976; Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Carrier Air Conditioning Philippines, Inc., G.R. No. 226592, July 27, 2021: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/67901
records.Controlling Doctrine: A judicial refund appeal filed before the statutory administrative period expires, and before denial, is premature.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Carrier Air Conditioning Philippines, Inc.

records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Topic: VAT Refund — Taxpayer’s Election
records.Essay Question: Fritzie Presley, Inc. (FPI) is a domestic corporation engaged in Value Added Tax (VAT) zero-rated transactions. In the second quarter of 2022, the input taxes of FPI from zero-rated sales amounted to PHP 9,811,152.02. The accountant of FPI advised to refund the input taxes and not to offset it with output taxes. On July 10, 2023, FPI filed a claim to refund the input taxes before the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) but was denied. FPI elevated the case to the Court of Tax Appeals (CTA). Meantime, the BIR’s assessment against FPI for deficiency output VAT for the second quarter of 2022 in the amount of PHP 8,501,355.53 became final and executory. After trial, the CTA granted FPI’s claim for refund but only for PHP 1,309,796.49 representing the difference between the excess input taxes and deficiency output taxes. The CTA held that since FPI has deficiency output taxes for 2022, the input taxes must first be applied against the deficiency taxes, and only the balance should be allowed for refund. On the other hand, FPI argued that the taxpayer-claimant has the option to charge the input taxes from zero-rated sales against the output taxes. May the CTA offset the input taxes against deficiency output taxes even without the taxpayer-claimant choosing this option? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The option to credit attributable input VAT or claim it for refund belongs to the taxpayer.

Legal Basis: Section 112(A) of the NIRC provides the alternative remedies for input VAT attributable to zero-rated sales. Chevron Holdings, Inc. v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue holds that the choice is vested in the taxpayer and that the CTA may not impose an offset the taxpayer did not elect.

Application: FPI chose to claim the qualifying input VAT for refund in its entirety. The CTA substituted a different remedy by crediting the amount against a separate final deficiency assessment.

Conclusion: The involuntary offset was improper, without prejudice to lawful collection of the final deficiency.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: NIRC, Section 112(A); Chevron Holdings, Inc. v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, G.R. No. 215159, July 5, 2022: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68508
records.Controlling Doctrine: The election to credit or refund input VAT attributable to zero-rated sales belongs to the taxpayer, not the CTA.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Chevron Holdings, Inc. v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue

records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Topic: Tax Prosecution — Civil Tax Liability After Acquittal
records.Essay Question: The Court of Tax Appeals (CTA) acquitted Stephen in a criminal case for non-filing of Annual Income Tax Return (ITR) under Section 255 of the Tax Code. The CTA ruled that the prosecution failed to prove Stephen’s guilt. However, the CTA imposed upon Stephen civil liability for deficiency income tax arising from the non-filing of ITR. Stephen questioned the civil aspect of the case and argued that his acquittal in the criminal case exonerated him from any civil liability arising from the offense. May the CTA impose civil liability to pay taxes upon Stephen despite his acquittal in the criminal case? Explain
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. The obligation to pay the tax arises from law and is not extinguished by failure to prove criminal guilt beyond reasonable doubt.

Legal Basis: Sections 205 and 255 of the NIRC allow tax collection and criminal prosecution. People v. Mendez holds that the civil action for tax recovery is jointly instituted and that unpaid tax is a statutory obligation, not merely civil liability ex delicto.

Application: Stephen’s acquittal means only that the prosecution failed to prove the criminal offense beyond reasonable doubt. It does not negate the tax assessment or the lower evidentiary basis for the collection component.

Conclusion: The CTA may order payment of the established deficiency tax despite acquittal.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: NIRC, Sections 205 and 255; People v. Mendez, G.R. Nos. 208310-11 and 208662, March 28, 2023: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/69095
records.Controlling Doctrine: Unpaid tax is an obligation created by law and may be recovered in the criminal tax case even when criminal guilt is not established.

records.Subject: Taxation Law
records.Topic: Tax Assessment — Letter of Authority
records.Essay Question: On June 30, 2023, the Commissioner of Internal Revenue (CIR) served a Letter of Authority (LOA) to Waldorf Weston Corporation (WWC). The LOA authorized Revenue Officer (RO) Arjun and Group Supervisor (GS) Simone to examine WWC’s accounting books and records for the taxable year 2021. Thereafter, WWC received a Memorandum-Referral Letter signed by Revenue District Officer (RDO) Desmond authorizing RO Valerie and GS Warren to continue the audit investigation. The memorandum noted that RO Arjun and GS Simone were already reassigned to another district office. After proper issuance of a Notice of Discrepancy and Preliminary Assessment Notice, RO Valerie and GS Warren jointly recommended that the CIR issue a Final Assessment Notice (FAN) against WWC because it had unreported gain subject to income tax for 2021. The CIR adopted the recommendation and served a FAN upon WWC. Aggrieved, WWC challenged the validity of the Memorandum-Referral Letter on the ground that it is not equivalent to a LOA. Is the Memorandum-Referral Letter valid to examine WWC’s accounting books and records? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. An internal referral cannot substitute for a new or amended LOA issued by an authorized official.

Legal Basis: Sections 6 and 13 of the NIRC require a valid LOA identifying the revenue officers empowered to examine the taxpayer. Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. McDonald’s Philippines Realty Corp. and Medicard Philippines, Inc. v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue hold that memoranda of assignment or referral do not confer audit authority.

Application: The original LOA named Arjun and Simone, not Valerie and Warren. Desmond’s internal memorandum neither amended the LOA through the proper authority nor independently supplied statutory power.

Conclusion: The continued examination and resulting assessment were unauthorized and void.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: NIRC, Sections 6 and 13; Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. McDonald’s Philippines Realty Corp., G.R. No. 242670, May 10, 2021: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/67422
records.Controlling Doctrine: Only a duly issued LOA can authorize named revenue officers to examine a taxpayer; an internal referral memorandum is not an LOA.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. McDonald’s Philippines Realty Corp.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Topic: Condition Precedent — Earnest Efforts Between Family Members
records.Essay Question: Gomez died leaving his wife Morticia and daughter Wednesday. Thereafter, Morticia filed a petition for probate of Gomez’s holographic will before the Regional Trial Court (RTC). The holographic will contained a detailed distribution of Gomez’s estate. Wednesday opposed the petition on the ground that it failed to allege that earnest efforts have been made among the surviving family members towards an amicable settlement of the estate of the deceased. The RTC dismissed the petition for probate absent compliance with a condition precedent as mandated by Article 151 of the Family Code. Is the RTC correct in dismissing the petition for probate for failure to allege earnest efforts toward a compromise? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The RTC was not correct.

Legal Basis: Article 151 of the Family Code applies to a suit between members of the same family. Vda. de Manalo v. Court of Appeals holds that the statutory earnest-efforts requirement applies only to ordinary civil actions, not to a special proceeding for settlement of an estate. Probate is also governed by the rule that a will passes no property unless proved and allowed in accordance with the Rules of Court.

Application: Morticia filed a probate proceeding to establish whether Gomez's holographic will should be allowed. It is a special proceeding, not an ordinary civil action by one family member against another. The absence of an allegation of prior earnest efforts therefore is not a condition precedent to the probate petition.

Conclusion: The RTC erred in dismissing the petition for probate on that ground.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Family Code, Article 151; Rules of Court, Rule 75, Section 1; Vda. de Manalo v. Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 129242, January 16, 2001: https://lawphil.net/judjuris/juri2001/jan2001/gr_129242_2001.html; Supreme Court E-Library: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/49760
records.Controlling Doctrine: The earnest-efforts requirement for intra-family suits applies only to ordinary civil actions; a proceeding for settlement of an estate, including probate, is a special proceeding and is not dismissible for failure to allege such efforts.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Vda. de Manalo v. Court of Appeals

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Topic: Res Judicata — Successive Unlawful Detainer Actions
records.Essay Question: Myrna leased her real property to Geybin for a period of one year. However, Geybin refused to vacate the premises after the expiration of the lease. Myrna then filed against Geybin an unlawful detainer case. The Metropolitan Trial Court (MeTC) ruled in favor of Myrna and ordered Geybin to surrender the real property. The judgment of the MeTC lapsed into finality but was not enforced. For humanitarian reasons, Myrna allowed Geybin to stay on the real property provided he will surrender its possession when needed. Thereafter, Myrna demanded from Geybin to vacate the premises but was refused. Myrna filed against Geybin another unlawful detainer case. In his answer, Geybin argued that the second ejectment case is barred by the prior final judgment in the first ejectment case. Does res judicata bar the institution of the second unlawful detainer case? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Res judicata does not bar the second unlawful-detainer case.

Legal Basis: Under Rule 39, Section 47(b), conclusiveness of judgment requires identity of the matters directly adjudged. Diaz, Jr. v. Valenciano, Jr. applies the same-evidence test to successive ejectment cases and recognizes that a later demand and breach under possession by tolerance may create a distinct cause of action.

Application: The first judgment in Myrna's favor arose from Geybin's refusal to vacate after the one-year lease expired. After that judgment became final, Myrna allowed him to remain for humanitarian reasons, subject to a new implied undertaking to surrender possession when demanded. His later refusal breached that new undertaking. Proof of the expired lease supported the first action; proof of the later tolerance, demand, and refusal supports the second.

Conclusion: The causes of action are distinct, so the second unlawful-detainer case is not barred.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Rules of Court, Rule 39, Section 47(b); Diaz, Jr. v. Valenciano, Jr., G.R. No. 209376, December 6, 2017: https://lawphil.net/judjuris/juri2017/dec2017/gr_209376_2017.html; Supreme Court E-Library: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/63625
records.Controlling Doctrine: Res judicata does not bar a later ejectment action when post-judgment tolerance and a new demand and refusal create a distinct cause of action requiring evidence different from the first action.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Diaz, Jr. v. Valenciano, Jr.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Topic: Search Warrants — Territorial Authority
records.Essay Question: The Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency (PDEA) received a tip from its confidential informant that Aidan was selling dangerous drugs in his residence in Quezon City. The PDEA agents conducted surveillance and confirmed the illegal activity. The PDEA agents then filed an application for search warrant before the Regional Trial Court (RTC) of Manila. The PDEA agents stated that Aidan has two kilos of shabu in his residence ready for disposal. The PDEA agents added that they will use two body-worn cameras. The Executive Judge of the RTC of Manila granted the application and issued a search warrant. The PDEA agents enforced the warrant and seized two kilos of shabu from Aidan. Is the issuance of search warrant valid? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The search warrant was not validly issued on the stated facts.

Legal Basis: Rule 126, Section 2(b) permits filing outside the court's territorial jurisdiction but within the same judicial region only for compelling reasons stated in the application. People v. Alagaban further requires those reasons to have an adequate evidentiary basis. The body-camera rules likewise require PDEA applications in special criminal cases to state compelling reasons for filing with the selected Executive Judge.

Application: The alleged drug activity and the place to be searched were in Quezon City, yet PDEA applied in Manila. The facts state no compelling reason for that choice and no substantiation for an exception. The proposed use of two body-worn cameras concerns execution of the warrant; it does not supply the missing compelling reason for venue.

Conclusion: On the facts given, the Manila RTC should not have issued the warrant.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Rules of Court, Rule 126, Section 2(b); Rules on the Use of Body-Worn Cameras in the Execution of Warrants, A.M. No. 21-06-08-SC, Rule 3, Section 2; People v. Alagaban, G.R. No. 244842, January 16, 2023: https://lawphil.net/judjuris/juri2023/jan2023/gr_244842_2023.html; Supreme Court E-Library: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/69061
records.Controlling Doctrine: An application filed in another court within the same judicial region must state and substantiate compelling reasons; absent an adequate basis, the application is insufficient and the warrant should not issue.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: People v. Alagaban

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Topic: Criminal Appeals — Optional Memorandum on Appeal
records.Essay Question: The Metropolitan Trial Court (MeTC) convicted Ivanka of theft and imposed upon her the indeterminate penalty of one year and eight months, as minimum, to three years, six months and 21 days, as maximum. Ivanka timely filed a notice of appeal. The MeTC then transmitted the records of the criminal case to the Regional Trial Court (RTC). Thereafter, the RTC directed Ivanka to file a memorandum of appeal. However, Ivanka failed to submit her memorandum despite notice. The RTC then dismissed Ivanka’s appeal for failure to file the required memorandum. Did the RTC properly dismiss Ivanka’s appeal for failure to file the required memorandum? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The RTC improperly dismissed Ivanka's appeal.

Legal Basis: Under Rule 122, Section 9(c), in an appeal from a first-level court to the RTC in a criminal case, the parties may submit memoranda, after which the RTC must decide the case on the entire record and any memoranda filed. Sanico v. People holds that the memorandum is optional in this appeal path.

Application: Ivanka timely perfected her criminal appeal by notice of appeal. Her failure to submit a memorandum did not authorize the RTC to dismiss it; the RTC should have resolved the appeal from the MeTC record, with or without her memorandum.

Conclusion: The dismissal must be set aside and the RTC must decide the appeal on the record.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Rules of Court, Rule 122, Section 9(c); Sanico v. People, G.R. No. 198753, March 25, 2015: https://lawphil.net/judjuris/juri2015/mar2015/gr_198753_2015.html; Supreme Court E-Library: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/59970
records.Controlling Doctrine: A memorandum on appeal is optional in a criminal appeal from a first-level court to the RTC; non-filing is not a ground to dismiss the appeal, which must be decided on the full record and any memoranda actually filed.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Topic: Child Witnesses — Out-of-Court Statement
records.Essay Question: Hermie and his 11-year old son Karter are residing in the province. Vincent, a talent manager, recruited Karter to be a child actor. Hermie agreed and gave parental consent. Vincent brought Karter in Manila. Vincent locked Karter in a small room and obliged him to have sex with clients. After one month, Vincent brought Karter inside an operating room and removed one of his corneas and a large portion of his skin. The operatives raided the premises, rescued Karter, and arrested Vincent. The social worker interviewed Karter who narrated how he was recruited, detained, sexually abused, and subjected to organ removal. The psychologist also diagnosed Karter with post-traumatic stress disorder. The prosecution charged Vincent with qualified human trafficking. However, Karter refused to testify because of severe trauma. At the trial, the prosecution called the social worker to the witness stand to establish the elements of the offense charged based on Karter’s statements during the interview. Vincent objected on the ground that the testimony of the social worker is inadmissible for being hearsay. Is the testimony of the social worker hearsay? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. The social worker's testimony is hearsay because it repeats Karter's out-of-court statements to prove the abuse and trafficking facts asserted. It may nevertheless be admitted under the special child-witness exception if its safeguards are met.

Legal Basis: Section 28 of the Rule on Examination of a Child Witness permits a child's hearsay statement describing child abuse when the adverse party receives the required notice, the court finds sufficient indicia of reliability, and the child testifies or is unavailable. Unavailability includes exposure to severe psychological injury; if the child is unavailable, the statement must be corroborated by other admissible evidence. People v. XXX258054 applies this doctrine, including to severe psychological injury, and discusses People v. BBB's application to qualified trafficking and post-traumatic stress disorder.

Application: Karter's statements were made outside court and are offered for their truth, so they are hearsay. His diagnosed post-traumatic stress disorder and refusal because of severe trauma can support a judicial finding of unavailability. Admissibility still requires the Section 28 notice, reliability findings, and corroboration shown at trial.

Conclusion: The testimony is hearsay, but the hearsay objection alone does not require exclusion if the prosecution establishes every applicable Section 28 safeguard.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Rule on Examination of a Child Witness, A.M. No. 004-07-SC, Section 28: https://lawphil.net/courts/supreme/am/am_004_07_sc_2000.html; People v. XXX258054, G.R. No. 258054, October 25, 2023: https://lawphil.net/judjuris/juri2023/oct2023/gr_258054_2023.html; Supreme Court E-Library: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/69604
records.Controlling Doctrine: A child's out-of-court abuse statement is hearsay, but it is admissible under Section 28 when notice and reliability requirements are met and the child either testifies or is unavailable; an unavailable child's statement also requires corroborating admissible evidence.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Topic: Death of a Party — Survival and Attachment
records.Essay Question: Esnyr filed against Fonzie a complaint for sum of money with prayer for preliminary attachment. Esnyr alleged that Fonzie failed to pay the consideration arising from their contract of service. The trial court granted the provisional remedy and levied Fonzie’s property. However, Fonzie died during the pendency of the proceedings. Accordingly, the heirs of Fonzie moved to dismiss the case and to dissolve the writ of preliminary attachment. The heirs of Fonzie argued that the writ of preliminary attachment would adversely affect their right to dispose the estate. The trial court dismissed the case and dissolved the writ of preliminary attachment. Did the trial court properly dismiss the case and dissolve the writ of preliminary attachment? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. A contractual money claim survives the defendant’s death, and a prior attachment is not automatically dissolved.

Legal Basis: Rule 3, Section 20 directs continuation of a contractual money action after the defendant’s death, followed by enforcement as a claim against the estate. Alipio v. Court of Appeals recognizes this procedure and the preservation of liens acquired before death.

Application: Esnyr’s action is contractual, and the attachment was obtained while Fonzie lived. The heirs’ desire to dispose of estate property is not itself a ground to dissolve the writ.

Conclusion: The action should continue through the proper legal representative, and the attachment remains unless dissolved on a ground provided by Rule 57.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Rules of Court, Rule 3, Section 20 and Rule 57; Alipio v. Court of Appeals: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/36251
records.Controlling Doctrine: A contractual money action survives death, and a lien acquired by attachment before death is preserved.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Topic: Electronic Evidence — Text Messages and Screenshots
records.Essay Question: Virgil filed a disbarment complaint against Atty. Flores for dishonest and deceitful conduct. Virgil alleged that he paid a substantial amount to Atty. Flores who promised to facilitate the release of a favorable judgment. The operatives then arrested Atty. Flores for selling fake court decisions. As supporting evidence, Virgil submitted screenshots of text messages exchanged between him and Atty. Flores, to wit: “If you send PHP 400,000.00 then you will surely win the case!”; “Atty ... I already deposited the amount, thank you.”; “Okay, received ... let’s wait for a month according to the judge.” However, Atty. Flores argued that the records are bereft of any proof showing that the text messages originated from a phone number registered in his name. Thus, the text messages are inadmissible in evidence. Are the text messages inadmissible in evidence? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The text messages are not inadmissible merely because the phone number was not proven to be registered in Atty. Flores's name.

Legal Basis: Text messages are ephemeral electronic communications under Rule 2, Section 1(k) of the Rules on Electronic Evidence. Under Rule 11, Section 2, they may be proved by the testimony of a party to the communication or a person with personal knowledge. Asuncion v. Salvado holds that a participant's testimony is sufficient to prove the contents of an exchanged text-message conversation.

Application: Virgil was a party to the exchange and can testify from personal knowledge about the messages he sent and received, their context, and the screenshots. Separate proof that the number was registered in Atty. Flores's name is not indispensable to admissibility when the exchange is authenticated through competent participant testimony.

Conclusion: Subject to Virgil's authentication and the ordinary rules on relevance and integrity, the text messages are admissible.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Rules on Electronic Evidence, Rule 2, Section 1(k), and Rule 11, Section 2; Asuncion v. Salvado, A.C. No. 13242, July 5, 2022: https://lawphil.net/judjuris/juri2022/jul2022/ac_13242_2022.html; Supreme Court E-Library: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68459
records.Controlling Doctrine: A participant to an ephemeral electronic communication may authenticate and prove it through personal-knowledge testimony; proof that the sender's number is formally registered in the sender's name is not invariably required.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Topic: Prejudicial Question — Criminal and Administrative Cases
records.Essay Question: Atty. Perez induced Eunice to invest money in a trading business with guaranteed profits. Atty. Perez assured Eunice that the business was doing well. Eunice agreed and delivered to Atty. Perez PHP 10,000,000.00 as capital investment. Atty. Perez issued to Eunice postdated checks with amounts representing her capital and expected profits. Thereafter, Eunice discovered that the trading business was a sham and that the checks were all drawn against a closed account. Aggrieved, Eunice filed against Atty. Perez a criminal action for estafa and a disbarment complaint for gross misconduct. Atty. Perez sought to suspend the disciplinary charge against him pending resolution of the criminal proceedings. Atty. Perez explained that his innocence or acquittal constitutes a prejudicial question to his administrative liability arising from similar incidents. Does the pending criminal action constitute a prejudicial question to warrant the suspension of the disbarment case? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. A prejudicial question exists only in the relationship between a previously filed civil action and a later criminal action, not between a criminal prosecution and a lawyer-disciplinary case.

Legal Basis: Rule 111, Section 7 states the elements of a prejudicial question. Wilson Po Cham v. Spouses Lim explains that an administrative disciplinary proceeding is independent and is not the civil action contemplated by the rule.

Application: The disbarment case concerns professional fitness under its own evidentiary standard and may proceed independently of criminal guilt.

Conclusion: The request to suspend the disciplinary proceeding should be denied.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Topic: Writ of Habeas Data — Scope
records.Essay Question: Colin is a strict team leader who earned the disdain and displeasure of his co-employees. Colin started to receive text messages and calls from unknown mobile numbers warning him that his days are numbered. Colin reported the threats to his manager. After investigation, the manager decided to transfer Colin to another station for security reasons. Colin repeatedly requested from his manager to disclose the details of the investigation but was refused. Aggrieved, Colin filed a petition for issuance of writ of habeas data to stop his involuntary transfer to another station which allegedly amounts to constructive dismissal. Colin also claimed that the unjustified refusal of the management to disclose the basis of his transfer constitutes serious threat to his rights to privacy and liberty. Will the petition for habeas data prosper to protect Colin’s right to security of tenure? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Habeas data protects informational privacy connected with life, liberty, or security; it is not a remedy for security of tenure or ordinary personnel disputes.

Legal Basis: Section 1 of the Rule on the Writ of Habeas Data defines its limited reach. Gamboa v. Chan holds that the writ does not issue without a concrete nexus between data gathering and a threat to life, liberty, or security.

Application: Colin’s complaint seeks reversal of a transfer and restoration to office. The facts show no qualifying threat to life, liberty, or security from unlawful data processing.

Conclusion: The petition should be dismissed without prejudice to the appropriate administrative or civil remedy.

records.Controlling Doctrine: Habeas data is confined to informational privacy violations that threaten life, liberty, or security.

records.Subject: Legal and Judicial Ethics
records.Topic: Legal Ethics — Delegation to Nonlawyer
records.Essay Question: Atty. Cassandra, a solo legal practitioner, hired Sandro as a legal researcher. Atty. Cassandra has an appeal brief due on September 25, 2024. However, Atty. Cassandra contracted monkeypox and suffered high fever, severe headache, and muscle fatigue. Atty. Cassandra then instructed Sandro to finish the appeal brief, affix her signature, and file the pleading with the Court of Appeals. Did Atty. Cassandra violate any provision of the Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. Atty. Cassandra violated the prohibition against delegating legal tasks that only a lawyer may perform.

Legal Basis: Canon II, Section 35 of the Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability prohibits a lawyer from delegating to, or permitting, a nonlawyer to perform independently a task that by law may be performed only by a member of the Bar. Under Rule 7, a counsel's signature certifies that counsel read the pleading and that it has proper legal and factual grounds. Petelo v. Rivera holds that preparing and signing a pleading are legal work reserved to lawyers and that counsel may not delegate the signature to a nonlawyer.

Application: Sandro is a legal researcher, not a lawyer. Cassandra instructed him to finish the appeal brief, affix her signature, and file it. Her illness may justify seeking an extension or arranging qualified counsel, but it does not authorize a nonlawyer to independently prepare and sign an appellate pleading in her name.

Conclusion: Cassandra violated CPRA Canon II, Section 35 and remained personally responsible for the improper delegation.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability, Canon II, Section 35; Rules of Court, Rule 7, Section 3; Petelo v. Rivera, A.C. No. 10408, October 16, 2019: https://lawphil.net/judjuris/juri2019/oct2019/ac_10408_2019.html; Supreme Court E-Library: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/65860
records.Controlling Doctrine: Preparation and signature of a pleading are professional legal acts; a lawyer may not authorize a nonlawyer to perform them independently or to affix the lawyer's signature.
records.Jurisprudence / Case: Petelo v. Rivera

records.Subject: Legal and Judicial Ethics
records.Topic: Legal Ethics — Communication with Represented Adverse Party
records.Essay Question: Francis, through Atty. Kyle, charged Madam Toyoh with violation of Presidential Decree No. 1612 or the Anti-Fencing Law for purchasing a vintage vehicle knowing that it proceeds from the crime of carnapping. Madam Toyoh hired Atty. Caleb as counsel and confessed to him that she is guilty of the offense. Atty. Caleb promised Madam Toyoh that he will do anything to prove her innocence. Atty. Caleb then reached out to Francis and negotiated for an amicable settlement that resulted in the execution of a release, quitclaim, and waiver of rights. Atty. Kyle discovered the compromise agreement and noticed some unfair provisions. Atty. Kyle filed against Atty. Caleb an administrative case for impropriety. On the other hand, Atty. Caleb countered that the ethical standards in the legal profession mandates lawyers to encourage clients to avoid or settle any controversy. Atty. Caleb added that the compromise agreement is beneficial to both parties. Did Atty. Caleb violate any provision of the Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. Atty. Caleb violated the CPRA by bypassing the represented adverse party's counsel and by securing an apparently unfair settlement from a nonlawyer.

Legal Basis: Canon II, Section 24 of the Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability prohibits a lawyer from attempting to communicate, negotiate, or deal with a person represented by another lawyer on the matter, unless the client initiated the contact or the person's lawyer knew of it. Canon II, Section 22 prohibits taking advantage of a nonlawyer's lack of legal knowledge. Canon III, Section 8 encourages settlement only when the matter can legally be compromised and admits of a fair settlement. Cabalida v. Lobrido, Jr. and Pondevilla disciplined a lawyer who negotiated a compromise directly with a party whom the lawyer knew was represented.

Application: Caleb knew from the case that Francis was represented by Atty. Kyle, yet Caleb directly reached out to Francis and negotiated the release, quitclaim, and waiver without any stated initiation by Francis or knowledge of Kyle. The provisions were later noticed to be unfair. Caleb's general duty to encourage settlement does not excuse bypassing counsel or obtaining an unfair compromise.

Conclusion: Caleb violated Canon II, Sections 24 and 22; the settlement policy in Canon III, Section 8 is not a defense on these facts.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability, Canon II, Sections 22 and 24, and Canon III, Section 8; Cabalida v. Lobrido, Jr. and Pondevilla, A.C. No. 7972, October 3, 2018: https://lawphil.net/judjuris/juri2018/oct2018/ac_7972_2018.html; Supreme Court E-Library: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/64657
records.Controlling Doctrine: A lawyer must not bypass opposing counsel to negotiate directly with a represented person unless the client initiated the contact or that person's lawyer knew of it; the duty to encourage compromise extends only to lawful and fair settlements.

records.Subject: Legal and Judicial Ethics
records.Topic: Legal Ethics — Online Misconduct During Suspension
records.Essay Question: Atty. Diwata, a suspended lawyer, created a professional social media page and maintained poser accounts which she used across various social networks. Atty. Diwata, during her livestream, spread fake news that the Court’s Strategic Plan for Judicial Innovations 2022-2027 failed to achieve its major target outcomes and had prejudiced the legal profession. Particularly, Atty. Diwata launched a social media campaign against the Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability and claimed that it is akin to an ex post facto law because its provisions are given retroactive effect. May the Supreme Court discipline Atty. Diwata for her social media activities? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. Suspension does not end a lawyer’s membership in the Bar or duty to maintain the profession’s standards, and the current disciplinary code applies to pending and future proceedings when fair and practicable.

Legal Basis: The Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability governs responsible social-media use and permits its procedural application under its general provisions. Supreme Court rulings on disturbing social-media posts recognize that online falsehoods and abuse may demonstrate unfitness to remain a lawyer.

Application: Diwata remained a lawyer while suspended and allegedly used deception to attack the justice system. The conduct bears directly on honesty and fitness.

Conclusion: Diwata may receive additional discipline after due process.

records.Controlling Doctrine: A suspended lawyer remains subject to discipline for dishonest online conduct that reflects unfitness for membership in the Bar.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Topic: Joinder of Parties — Misjoinder
records.Essay Question: Pauline and Regine had a dispute over a 500-square meter parcel of land that they inherited from their deceased parents, Milcah and James. During the barangay conciliation proceedings, both Pauline and Regine agreed to partition the lot in equal shares. As a result, the title to the property was cancelled and new titles were issued in favor of Pauline and Regine as to their respective lots. However, Regine discovered that the lot covered by her title was on the eastern portion rather than the northern portion, contrary to their agreement. Hence, Regine filed a “Petition for Annulment of Transfer Certificate of Title (TCT) and Barangay Partition, with Prayer for Judicial Partition of the Intestate Estate of the Spouses Milcah and James” against Pauline. After trial, the court rendered judgment in favor of Regine. Pauline then consulted a newly-minted lawyer, Atty. Terry, who explained to her that there was a misjoinder of causes of action when Regine included both annulment of TCT and the barangay partition, as well as judicial partition in the petition. Hence, the trial court erred when it ruled on both causes of action instead of dismissing the petition of Regine. Is Atty. Terry correct? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Misjoinder is not a ground to dismiss the action.

Legal Basis: Rule 3, Section 11 directs the court to drop or add parties, or sever claims, on just terms. Ada v. Baylon holds that procedural misjoinder should be corrected rather than used to defeat the entire suit.

Application: The unrelated party or claim may be dropped or separately tried without extinguishing Pauline’s properly joined partition claim.

Conclusion: The motion to dismiss the whole complaint should be denied, with severance or dropping of the misjoined matter as appropriate.

records.Controlling Doctrine: Misjoinder of parties or causes does not warrant dismissal; the court should drop or sever the improper matter.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Topic: Depositions — Prosecution Witness Abroad
records.Essay Question: Clarisse and Myra offered Gaita a job as a domestic helper in Indonesia. Clarisse gave Gaita her plane ticket and luggage to bring on her trip. Upon reaching the airport of Yogyakarta, Indonesia, she was apprehended by the police for allegedly carrying two kilograms of heroin inside her luggage. She was then charged before the Indonesian courts with drug trafficking, and subsequently convicted and sentenced to death by firing squad. Meanwhile, in the Philippines, Clarisse and Myra were arrested and charged with Qualified Trafficking of Persons, Illegal Recruitment, and Estafa in the Regional Trial Court (RTC) of Angeles City. Gaita was given an indefinite reprieve by the Indonesian Government to give her the opportunity to testify in the case against Clarisse and Myra. Hence, the People of the Philippines, through the Office of the Solicitor General (OSG), filed a motion to take the testimony of Gaita upon written interrogatories under Rule 23 (Deposition Pending Action) of the Rules of Court. The RTC granted the motion of the OSG. Was the action of the RTC proper? Discuss your answer.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The prosecution cannot substitute a foreign deposition on written interrogatories for the personal examination required in a Philippine criminal case.

Legal Basis: Rule 119, Section 15 permits conditional examination of a prosecution witness only before the court where the case is pending. Go v. People, discussing People v. Sergio, distinguishes this from the accused’s conditional examination and protects confrontation.

Application: Myra would be examined abroad, outside the trial court’s supervision, and by written questions that prevent effective contemporaneous cross-examination.

Conclusion: The proposed prosecution deposition should be denied.

records.Controlling Doctrine: A prosecution witness’s conditional examination must occur before the court where the criminal case is pending.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Topic: Amendment of Information — Name Suffix
records.Essay Question: William and several other persons were charged with violation of the Anti-Hazing Act. During their arraignment, William and his co-accused pleaded not guilty to the charge that they unlawfully subjected Carding Cruz to hazing. The information was later amended by adding the suffix “III” to the name “Carding Cruz”. Trial ensued without the accused having been re-arraigned on the amended information. After the accused were convicted by the trial court, William appealed contending that his right to be informed of the nature and cause of the accusation against him was violated when he was not re-arraigned after the amendment of the information. Is William correct? Discuss.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. William is not correct.

Legal Basis: Under Rule 110, Section 14, after plea and during trial a formal amendment may be made with leave of court if it does not prejudice the accused. Villarba v. Court of Appeals holds that a formal amendment which does not change the offense, the prosecution's theory, or the defense does not require a second arraignment.

Application: Adding the suffix "III" merely states Carding Cruz's name with greater precision. It does not change the Anti-Hazing Act charge, any element of the offense, the person referred to, or the defense available to William.

Conclusion: The amendment was formal, re-arraignment was unnecessary, and William's right to be informed was not violated.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Rules of Court, Rule 110, Section 14; Villarba v. Court of Appeals: https://lawphil.net/judjuris/juri2020/jun2020/gr_227777_2020.html; Supreme Court E-Library: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/66301
records.Controlling Doctrine: A post-plea amendment is formal when it merely states with additional precision what the information already contains and does not change the crime, prosecution theory, available defense, or substantial rights; a formal amendment does not require a second arraignment.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Topic: Bail — Application Pending Appeal
records.Essay Question: Angel was charged with Murder before the Regional Trial Court (RTC). After trial, the court convicted her of Homicide due to the absence of the qualifying circumstance of treachery. She then filed a notice of appeal and applied for bail with the RTC before transmittal of the records to the Court of Appeals. The prosecution opposed the application, contending that the RTC has no jurisdiction to act on the application for bail. The RTC granted the application for bail on the ground that the prosecution failed to prove the five bail-negating circumstances. Did the RTC have jurisdiction to act on the application for bail filed by Angel? Discuss your answer.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The RTC had no jurisdiction to resolve Angel's application for bail.

Legal Basis: Rule 114, Section 5 generally allows the trial court to act on bail after notice of appeal but before transmission of the original record. The same provision expressly creates an exception: when conviction changes the offense from non-bailable to bailable, the application may be filed with and resolved only by the appellate court. Leviste v. Court of Appeals applies this exception.

Application: Angel was charged with Murder, a non-bailable offense when the evidence of guilt is strong, but was convicted of Homicide, a bailable offense. That change brings the case within the express exception even though the record had not yet been transmitted. The five bail-negating circumstances guide the appellate court's discretion; their absence cannot give the RTC authority that the rule withholds.

Conclusion: Only the Court of Appeals could act on Angel's application for bail pending appeal.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Rules of Court, Rule 114, Section 5; Leviste v. Court of Appeals: https://lawphil.net/judjuris/juri2010/mar2010/gr_189122_2010.html; Supreme Court E-Library: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/53777
records.Controlling Doctrine: When the judgment of conviction changes the offense from non-bailable to bailable, exclusive authority to file and resolve bail pending appeal lies with the appellate court, even before transmittal of the original record.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Topic: Warrants of Arrest — Execution Period
records.Essay Question: On October 18, 2021, a warrant of arrest was issued against Erica. At 11:00 p.m. on October 30, 2021, police officers arrested Erica at her house pursuant to the arrest warrant. Before arraignment, Erica moved to quash the information on the grounds that the warrant was served at nighttime and beyond ten days from its issuance. Is the position of Erica tenable? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The ten-day period governs the officer’s duty to report, not the warrant’s validity.

Legal Basis: Rule 113, Section 4 requires the officer to execute the warrant within ten days from receipt and report the result, but an arrest warrant remains effective until executed, recalled, or quashed. Manangan v. Cudia confirms that it does not become stale merely through lapse of time.

Application: The officer’s failure to serve or report within ten days may call for explanation or sanction, but it does not cancel the judicial command.

Conclusion: The warrant may still be executed unless the issuing court recalls or quashes it.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Rules of Court, Rule 113, Section 4; Manangan v. Cudia, G.R. No. 82760: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/assets/pdf/philrep/1990/G.R.%20No.%2082760.pdf
records.Controlling Doctrine: An arrest warrant does not expire after ten days; that period concerns execution reporting.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Topic: Informations — Prosecutor Approval
records.Essay Question: An information for Corruption of Public Officials was filed against Bel. Assistant City Prosecutor Chi, the investigating prosecutor, certified in the information that the same was filed with the prior authority of Jill, the City Prosecutor. After the presentation of evidence by both parties, the trial court motu proprio dismissed the case on the ground that Chi does not have the authority to prosecute the case because the information does not bear the signature of Jill or any other indication that she approved the same. The trial court explained that the lack of authority to file an information is a jurisdictional defect that cannot be cured. Is the trial court correct? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The trial court is not correct.

Legal Basis: Rule 112, Section 4 requires prior written authority or approval for an investigating prosecutor to file an information. Under Rule 117, Sections 3(d) and 9, lack of authority is a ground to quash that is waived if not raised before plea. Villa Gomez v. People holds that absence of the approving officer's signature or approval on the face of the information is not a defect in subject-matter or personal jurisdiction; authority may also be established by the record.

Application: Chi certified that Jill had given prior authority. The case proceeded through the presentation of both parties' evidence without a timely motion to quash. The trial court could not treat the missing signature on the information as an incurable jurisdictional defect and dismiss the case motu proprio after trial.

Conclusion: The dismissal was improper; the case should be reinstated for adjudication on the merits.

records.Controlling Doctrine: The absence on the face of an information of the approving prosecutor's signature or written approval does not deprive the trial court of subject-matter or personal jurisdiction. Lack of filing authority is a waivable ground to quash, and authority may be shown by the record.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Topic: Evidence — Competency of a Child Witness
records.Essay Question: Raisa filed a case for support against Ton on behalf of their 9-year-old daughter, Rox. During trial, Rox was presented as a witness. The counsel of Ton invoked the rule on the incompetence of Rox to testify against her father given her tender age. The trial court allowed Rox to testify. Is the trial court correct? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. The trial court is correct.

Legal Basis: Rule 130, Section 21 allows all persons who can perceive and can make known their perception to testify. Section 6 of the Rule on Examination of a Child Witness presumes every child qualified; only substantial doubt about the child's ability to perceive, remember, communicate, distinguish truth from falsehood, or appreciate the duty to tell the truth warrants a competency examination. Esugon v. People confirms that age alone does not disqualify a child witness and places the burden on the challenger.

Application: Ton relied only on Rox's tender age. At nine years old, Rox is not automatically incompetent, and no fact shows substantial doubt as to the relevant abilities.

Conclusion: The court properly allowed Rox to testify, subject to the ordinary assessment of competence and credibility.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Rules on Evidence, Rule 130, Section 21; Rule on Examination of a Child Witness, Section 6; Esugon v. People: https://lawphil.net/judjuris/juri2015/jun2015/gr_195244_2015.html; Supreme Court E-Library: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/60772
records.Controlling Doctrine: Every child is presumed qualified to testify; age alone is not disqualifying, and the party challenging competency must show substantial doubt about the child's ability to perceive, remember, communicate, distinguish truth from falsehood, or understand the duty to tell the truth.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Topic: Evidence — Corpus Delicti, Missing Weapon or Body, and Paraffin Test
records.Essay Question: In a criminal case for Murder filed against Erika, the prosecution presented Chelle as an eyewitness to the killing of Ly. Chelle testified that while the three of them were on board a boat, Erika shot Ly with a .45 caliber pistol and threw both the gun and the body of Ly into the sea. Efforts to retrieve the gun and the body of Ly were unsuccessful. Evidence was likewise introduced to prove that Ly was thrown in a shark-infested area. Erika consulted her nephew, Ted, a recent law school graduate who is reviewing for the Bar examinations. Confident of an acquittal, Ted recommended that Erika file a demurrer to evidence because: 1) there is no corpus delicti due to the failure to recover the gun and the body of Ly; and 2) the prosecution failed to prove that Erika fired the gun due to the lack of a paraffin test. Is Ted correct? Discuss.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Ted is not correct.

Legal Basis: Corpus delicti requires proof that a certain result occurred and that someone is criminally responsible for it. People v. Pitulan y Briones holds that the murder weapon is not an element and need not be produced when credible eyewitness testimony proves the crime and identifies the assailant. It also holds that paraffin testing is inconclusive as to the source of nitrates and is not indispensable where there is a credible eyewitness.

Application: Chelle testified that she personally saw Erika shoot Ly and throw both Ly's body and the gun into a shark-infested area. If found credible, that direct eyewitness testimony may establish Ly's death, criminal agency, and Erika's identity despite the unsuccessful recovery efforts. The lack of a paraffin test does not negate Chelle's positive identification.

Conclusion: The two grounds proposed by Ted do not warrant a demurrer; the court must assess whether Chelle's testimony and the remaining evidence prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Rules of Court, Rule 133, Section 2; People v. Pitulan y Briones: https://lawphil.net/judjuris/juri2020/jan2020/gr_226486_2020.html; Supreme Court E-Library: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/21/66100
records.Controlling Doctrine: The body and murder weapon are not indispensable when credible evidence proves the victim's death, criminal agency, and the accused's identity. Paraffin testing is inconclusive as to the source of nitrates and is not indispensable when a credible eyewitness positively identifies the shooter.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Topic: Hearsay Exceptions — Pedigree
records.Essay Question: Vangie filed an action for compulsory recognition with prayer for support against Jay, her putative father. During trial, she presented and identified the following documents on the witness stand: 1) the birth certificate of Vangie reflecting Jay as the father of Vangie per information supplied by the mother of Vangie, but was unsigned by Jay; and 2) letters from the siblings of Jay, addressed to private schools where Vangie was enrolled, which attested that Jay is the father of Vangie and that he regularly supports her education. Rule on the admissibility and sufficiency of the documents as evidence of acts or declarations about pedigree. Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No, not on the stated foundation.

Legal Basis: Rule 130, Sections 39 and 40 require the declarant’s unavailability, qualifying family relationship or intimate association, and a declaration made before the controversy. Jison v. Court of Appeals enforces these prerequisites for pedigree evidence.

Application: Vangie did not prove the declarants’ unavailability, relationship, or ante litem motam character. A document’s existence does not itself satisfy the hearsay exception.

Conclusion: The birth certificate and letters cannot be admitted under the asserted pedigree exception unless the missing foundation is supplied or another rule independently permits admission.

records.Subject: Legal and Judicial Ethics
records.Topic: Legal Ethics — Practice During Suspension
records.Essay Question: The Supreme Court suspended Atty. Irish for one year in an administrative case filed against her for Gross Misconduct. During the effectivity of her suspension, Janet appointed her as attorney-in-fact in an execution sale arising from a civil case that she previously handled. At the execution sale, Atty. Irish took part in the bidding and negotiations as regards the payment of the judgment award. Atty. Elvie, the opposing counsel in the civil case, questioned the appearance by Atty. Irish during the execution sale because of her suspension. Atty. Irish argued that she was merely acting as an attorney-in-fact of Janet, which was not tantamount to the practice of law. Do you agree with Atty. Irish? Explain your answer.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. I do not agree with Atty. Irish.

Legal Basis: Practice of law includes services requiring a trained legal mind to determine the legal effects and consequences of a course of action; it is not confined to courtroom appearances. Under Rule 138, Section 27, willful disobedience of a lawful court order is ground for discipline. Bonifacio v. Era holds that a suspended lawyer who represents clients in an execution sale and negotiates satisfaction of the judgment is practicing law and cannot evade suspension through a special power of attorney.

Application: Atty. Irish acted in the execution of a case she had handled, took part in bidding, and negotiated payment of the judgment award for Janet. Those acts called for legal judgment and advanced Janet's rights in the execution proceeding. Her appointment as attorney-in-fact does not alter their legal character.

Conclusion: Atty. Irish engaged in unauthorized practice during her suspension and may be subjected to further discipline.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Rules of Court, Rule 138, Section 27; Bonifacio v. Era: https://lawphil.net/judjuris/juri2017/oct2017/ac_11754_2017.html; Supreme Court E-Library: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/63537
records.Controlling Doctrine: A suspended lawyer cannot evade a suspension order by acting under a special power of attorney when the acts require a trained legal mind and constitute representation in the execution and settlement of a judgment.

records.Subject: Legal and Judicial Ethics
records.Topic: Judicial Discipline — Ombudsman Jurisdiction
records.Essay Question: Romy filed an administrative complaint against Judge Ferdie with the Office of the Ombudsman in relation to the Bribery he allegedly committed as a Presiding Judge of a Regional Trial Court. After investigation, the Ombudsman found him guilty of Grave Misconduct and imposed the penalty of dismissal from service. May the Ombudsman dismiss Judge Ferdie? Explain.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Administrative supervision and discipline of judges belong exclusively to the Supreme Court.

Legal Basis: Article VIII, Section 6 of the Constitution vests administrative supervision over all courts and personnel in the Supreme Court. Maceda v. Vasquez and Office of the Ombudsman v. Judge Dolalas require complaints implicating judicial duties to be referred to the Court.

Application: The charge against Judge Ferdie concerns judicial conduct. The Ombudsman cannot impose removal without intruding on the Court’s exclusive constitutional authority.

Conclusion: The dismissal order is void; the matter must be referred to the Supreme Court, without prejudice to any distinct criminal investigation within lawful bounds.

records.Subject: Legal and Judicial Ethics
records.Topic: Practical Exercise — Deed of Absolute Sale
records.Essay Question: Edsel A. Flores, a resident of Bacoor City, Cavite, sold to Joel R. Vargas, a resident of Binondo, Manila, a parcel of land located in Bacoor City, Cavite. The parcel of land had an area of 500 square meters, and was covered by a clean Original Certificate of Title No. 1234567 issued by the Registry of Deeds of Cavite. The purchase price amounts to ₱8 million. The parties agreed that the seller shall bear the capital gains tax, real estate tax, and documentary stamp tax, while the buyer shall bear the rest of the expenses. Prepare a notarized deed of absolute sale.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: The requested notarizable instrument may be drafted as follows.

Legal Basis: Articles 1358, 1458, and 1475 of the Civil Code govern the form and perfection of a sale of immovable property. The 2004 Rules on Notarial Practice require personal appearance, competent evidence of identity, and a complete acknowledgment and notarial certificate.

Application: The deed below uses only the facts supplied in the question. It leaves blank every unstated identity, date, civil-status, technical-description, and notarial-commission particular instead of inventing a fact.

Conclusion: Subject to completing the bracketed particulars and inserting the exact title description, the following instrument supplies the requested deed and acknowledgment.

DEED OF ABSOLUTE SALE

KNOW ALL PERSONS BY THESE PRESENTS:

This Deed of Absolute Sale is made and executed by EDSEL A. FLORES, [age, citizenship, and civil status], and a resident of Bacoor City, Cavite, hereinafter called the "SELLER";

— in favor of —

JOEL R. VARGAS, [age, citizenship, and civil status], and a resident of Binondo, Manila, hereinafter called the "BUYER."

WITNESSETH:

WHEREAS, the SELLER is the registered owner of a parcel of land situated in Bacoor City, Cavite, containing an area of FIVE HUNDRED (500) SQUARE METERS, covered by clean Original Certificate of Title No. 1234567 issued by the Registry of Deeds of Cavite, and more particularly described in that title as follows:

The SELLER warrants that he has lawful title to and authority to convey the property and that Original Certificate of Title No. 1234567 is clean and free from liens and encumbrances. The SELLER shall defend the BUYER's title against lawful claims arising from acts attributable to the SELLER.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Topic: Summons — Substituted Service
records.Essay Question:
Asya, Inc. sued Kobe, a resident of Bukidnon. To serve summons, the sheriff waited in the lobby of Makati Hotel (MH), where Kobe stays whenever he is in Manila. The sheriff failed to serve the summons because Kobe left the hotel for an emergency. Hours later, the sheriff asked the front desk about Kobe’s whereabouts and his room number. The hotel refused to disclose on grounds of confidentiality. The sheriff tried again the next day, but Kobe was in a conference until midnight. So, the following day, the sheriff left the summons and a copy of the complaint with MH's chief security officer (CSO), even as the CSO refused because Kobe had already checked out by then. The sheriff thereafter filed his return, stating the dates, times and places of his attempts, the name of the CSO, and the fact that the complaint was served with the summons. When Kobe did not file an Answer, Asya, Inc. moved to declare him in default.

Was there a valid substituted service of summons? Explain briefly. (5 points)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Substituted service is exceptional and requires strict proof of prior diligent personal-service attempts and delivery at a place and to a person authorized by the rule.

Legal Basis: Rule 14, Section 6 requires personal service whenever practicable; substituted service under Section 7 is allowed only for justifiable causes and prescribed recipients. Manotoc v. Court of Appeals demands a detailed sheriff’s return showing compliance.

Application: A temporary hotel and its receptionist were not shown to be Kobe’s residence, regular business, or authorized recipient, and the return did not establish diligent prior attempts.

Conclusion: The substituted service was invalid.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Topic: Summons — Affirmative Defense
records.Essay Question:
Ten days after service of summons, defendant Kay filed a motion to dismiss the complaint for collection of sum of money against her on the ground of improper service of summons, on the basis of which the court did not acquire jurisdiction over her person.

If you were the judge, how would you rule? Explain briefly. (5 points)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: The court should not grant a prohibited stand-alone motion to dismiss, but Kay may preserve lack of jurisdiction over her person as an affirmative defense in the answer.

Legal Basis: Rule 15, Section 12 generally prohibits motions to dismiss except for specified grounds, while Rule 8, Section 12 requires affirmative defenses, including lack of personal jurisdiction, to be pleaded and resolved early. United Coconut Planters Bank v. Ongpin explains that voluntary appearance may confer personal jurisdiction except when made solely to object.

Application: Kay’s objection remains potentially valid, but the amended procedure requires it to be asserted through the answer unless it falls within an express motion exception.

Conclusion: The stand-alone motion should be denied without treating the jurisdictional objection as waived if Kay timely pleads it as an affirmative defense.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Topic: Filing and Service — Accredited Courier
records.Essay Question:
[This item has two questions.] Attorney Woo, the newly-hired lawyer of a law firm, booked Samurai Express, a duly accredited courier service within the National Capital Judicial Region, to serve a copy of a motion for reconsideration to Attorney Han, counsel for the adverse party, whose office is in the City of Manila. Attorney Han moved to deny the motion for failure to contain a written explanation as to why the motion was not served personally.

(a) Was the motion for reconsideration properly served? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes, if the courier was accredited and the service complied with Rule 13. The amended rules no longer require a written explanation merely because personal service was not used.

Legal Basis: Rule 13, Sections 5 and 6 expressly permit service and filing through accredited courier. IP E-Game Ventures, Inc. v. Tan discusses the governing modes and the effect of the amended procedural framework.

Application: Attorney Woo used a mode expressly authorized by the current rule. The former written-explanation requirement cannot be reintroduced when the amended text does not require it.

Conclusion: The courier service is valid upon compliance with the rule’s addressing and proof requirements.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Topic: Filing and Service — Proof by Accredited Courier
records.Essay Question:
[This item has two questions.] Attorney Woo, the newly-hired lawyer of a law firm, booked Samurai Express, a duly accredited courier service within the National Capital Judicial Region, to serve a copy of a motion for reconsideration to Attorney Han, counsel for the adverse party, whose office is in the City of Manila. Attorney Han moved to deny the motion for failure to contain a written explanation as to why the motion was not served personally.

(b) What shall be considered as proof of service of this motion? Explain briefly.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Proof consists of the sender’s affidavit of service together with the courier’s official receipt and tracking or delivery record, as required by Rule 13.

Legal Basis: Rule 13, Section 17 prescribes proof for service by accredited courier. Heirs of Deloy v. Court of Appeals illustrates the need for competent documentary proof of the chosen service mode.

Application: The affidavit should identify the pleading, addressee, date, place, and manner of deposit, while the courier records independently show acceptance and delivery tracking.

Conclusion: Samurai should retain and submit the affidavit, official receipt, and available tracking or delivery confirmation.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Topic: Res Judicata — Conclusiveness of Judgment
records.Essay Question:
Jimuel filed against his wife Jewel a petition for the declaration of nullity of their marriage, alleging as ground therefor Jewel’s psychological incapacity under Article 36 of the Family Code. The court denied the petition for insufficiency of the evidence presented at the trial. Much later, Jimuel again filed a petition against Jewel for the declaration of nullity of their marriage. This time, the basis of Jimuel’s petition was the absence of a marriage license at the time their marriage was celebrated. Upon Jewel's motion, the court dismissed the petition on the ground of res judicata by virtue of the judgment in the first suit.

Was the denial of the petition on the ground of res judicata proper? Explain briefly. (5 points)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes, to the extent the second petition seeks to relitigate the same finally determined marital-status issue.

Legal Basis: Rule 39, Section 47 embodies bar by prior judgment and conclusiveness of judgment. Dy v. Bibat-Palamos holds that a final adjudication binds the parties on matters directly resolved and cannot be evaded by changing theories.

Application: Jimuel and Jewel are the same parties, and the first final judgment determined the validity issue. A new label for substantially the same asserted defect does not reopen that adjudication.

Conclusion: The second petition should be dismissed under res judicata or conclusiveness of judgment, as the identity of causes and issues warrants.
records.Legal Basis / Provision: Rules of Court, Rule 39, Section 47; Dy v. Bibat-Palamos: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/61079
records.Controlling Doctrine: A final judgment binds the parties on issues actually and directly resolved, notwithstanding a later change in legal theory.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Topic: Provisional Remedies — Preliminary Injunction
records.Essay Question:
Isol, Inc. supplies rotisserie chicken products to the grocery section of shopping malls. It conducts kitchen operations in a refurbished house located in Palanan, a residential neighborhood. Rona, a resident of Palanan, filed an action against Isol, Inc. to enjoin the operations of its kitchen on the ground that it emits intolerable odors and violates laws on waste disposal. In the same action, Rona also seeks to have Isol, Inc.’s business permit revoked because an industrial facility is not allowed by law to be located in a residential neighborhood and Isol, Inc. failed to comply with sanitary inspection and other procedural and health requirements. In the complaint Rona filed, she likewise prayed for the issuance of a writ of preliminary injunction (WPI) to stop the kitchen operations during the pendency of the case. Isol, Inc., in its verified answer, strongly opposed the prayer for WPI considering the huge financial disaster that it will suffer if the writ were to be issued, especially in light of the possibility that the suit could continue to be pending for more than a year.

Based on the foregoing, may the WPI prayed for already be issued? Explain briefly. (5 points)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No, unless Isol proves a clear and unmistakable right, an urgent necessity, and irreparable injury that cannot be adequately compensated.

Legal Basis: Rule 58, Section 3 governs preliminary injunction. Cahambing v. Espinosa states that the remedy protects an existing right and cannot create one while title or entitlement remains doubtful.

Application: Isol’s asserted right to control the kitchen is itself disputed. Imminent alteration may show urgency, but urgency cannot replace proof of a clear right.

Conclusion: The application should be denied on the stated facts, without prejudice to renewed relief upon sufficient proof.

records.Controlling Doctrine: Preliminary injunction requires a clear existing right and urgent irreparable injury; it cannot establish a disputed right.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Topic: Succession — Action by Heirs Without Prior Declaration
records.Essay Question: Is a prior determination of the status as a legal heir in a separate special proceeding a prerequisite to an ordinary civil action seeking the protection and enforcement of ownership rights of such legal heir vested by the law of succession? Explain briefly. (5 points)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No.

Legal Basis: Article 777 of the Civil Code transmits successional rights from the moment of the decedent's death. Treyes v. Larlar holds that, unless a special proceeding for settlement of the estate or determination of heirship is already pending, compulsory or intestate heirs may bring an ordinary civil action to enforce ownership rights acquired by succession without a prior and separate judicial declaration of heirship.

Application: The action described seeks protection and enforcement of ownership rights that vested by succession, not a separate declaration of status. If no estate or heirship proceeding is pending, heirship may be addressed incidentally in the ordinary action and the ruling binds only the parties.

Conclusion: A prior separate determination of heirship is not a prerequisite in that circumstance.

records.Controlling Doctrine: Unless an estate-settlement or heirship proceeding is already pending, compulsory or intestate heirs may bring an ordinary civil action to enforce ownership rights acquired by succession without a prior separate declaration of heirship; the ruling binds only the parties to that action.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Topic: Special Proceedings — Recognition of Foreign Divorce
records.Essay Question:
Namjoon, a Korean national, and Regine, a Filipina, were married in Makati City on February 14, 2012. Unfortunately, their relationship shortly turned sour and ended with a divorce by mutual agreement in South Korea. The local court in Korea granted the divorce. Wanting to marry her new boyfriend Taehyung, Regine filed a petition for recognition of the foreign decree of divorce in the Regional Trial Court (RTC) of Cebu where she resides.

The Office of the Solicitor General (OSG) opposed the petition contending that the proper remedy is a special proceeding for cancellation or correction of entries in the civil registry under Rule 108 of the Rules of Court, which can only be filed in the RTC of Makati where the marriage was celebrated and recorded in the Civil Registry of Makati.

Is the OSG’s contention tenable? Explain briefly. (5 points)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. A foreign divorce may be recognized in a Rule 108 proceeding, filed in the Regional Trial Court of the province where the corresponding civil registry is located.

Legal Basis: Rule 108, Sections 1 and 2 govern cancellation or correction of civil-registry entries. Fujiki v. Marinay holds that recognition of a foreign judgment affecting civil status may be joined with correction proceedings, subject to proof of the judgment and foreign law.

Application: Regine seeks to annotate the marriage record based on Namjoon’s Korean divorce. She must prove the authentic divorce decree and applicable Korean law and implead the required parties.

Conclusion: The petition is procedurally proper in the RTC where the relevant civil registry is situated.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Topic: Ejectment — Binding Effect of Judgment
records.Essay Question:
Notting Hill Corp. filed an action for forcible entry against the ten occupants of a parcel of land it owns. After the summary proceedings, the Municipal Trial Court (MTC) rendered judgment against the ten defendants. The defendants filed a notice of appeal, but failed to file a supersedeas bond to stay the judgment to vacate. Upon Notting Hill Corp.’s motion, the MTC issued a writ of execution.

When Hugh, the sheriff, was implementing the writ of execution, he discovered that the land was occupied by a number of families who all claimed that they were legitimate lessees of the ten defendants. Julia, one of the lessees, pleaded with Hugh, beseeching: “I’m just a lessee, standing in front of a sheriff, asking him to let me stay in my home.”

May Hugh implement the writ of execution against the lessees? Explain briefly. (5 points)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes, if she entered under Hugh or derived possession from him after commencement of the action.

Legal Basis: Rule 39, Section 47 and the ejectment rules bind successors-in-interest and persons holding under the defendant. Heirs of Mariano v. City of Naga explains that a judgment may be enforced against privies whose possessory right is subordinate to the adjudged party.

Application: Julia’s occupation came through Hugh, so she has no independent possession superior to the judgment and cannot defeat execution by nonjoinder.

Conclusion: The writ may be enforced against Julia, subject to proof that she is in fact Hugh’s privy.

records.Controlling Doctrine: An ejectment judgment binds sublessees, transferees, and other privies holding under the losing defendant.

records.Subject: Remedial Law
records.Topic: Plea of Guilty — Capital Offense
records.Essay Question:
Cain was indicted under an Information charging him with the crime of Murder. He was caught by the police in flagrante delicto as the incident happened in a public place with many witnesses present. Videos of the incident were also posted online which the judge was able to watch.

During his arraignment, Cain pleaded guilty to the crime charged. The Regional Trial Court (RTC) accepted the plea because it was made voluntarily and with full understanding of the consequences. The RTC directed the prosecution to present evidence to prove Cain’s guilt. However, the prosecution failed to present any evidence during the scheduled hearings. The RTC then ruled and found Cain guilty beyond reasonable doubt based solely on his plea of guilt.

Was Cain’s conviction proper? Explain briefly. (5 points)
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. For a capital offense, the court must conduct a searching inquiry, require prosecution evidence, and allow the accused to present evidence despite the guilty plea.

Legal Basis: Rule 116, Section 3 makes these safeguards mandatory. People v. Pagal reiterates that a guilty plea does not relieve the prosecution of proving guilt and the precise degree of culpability.

Application: The court skipped the prosecution-evidence stage and based judgment solely on Cain’s plea.

Conclusion: The judgment is procedurally defective and must be set aside for compliance with Rule 116.
