records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Peaceful Concerted Activities - see also R.A. No. 6727 — Strikes
records.Essay Question: A union staged a strike before completing the required seven-day waiting period after submitting its strike-vote report. Union officer Ramon planned the stoppage and led the picket. Ordinary member Liza joined after being told all requirements were complete; she committed no violence or other unlawful act. The employer dismissed both solely because the strike was illegal. Are the same employment consequences proper for Ramon and Liza? The termination notices identify no violent act by Liza and rely entirely on the illegality of the stoppage, while meeting minutes confirm Ramon helped choose the premature date.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. A union officer who knowingly participates in an illegal strike may be dismissed, while an ordinary member requires proof of a separate illegal act.

Legal Basis: Hongkong & Shanghai Banking Corp. Employees Union v. NLRC and CCBPI Postmix Workers Union v. NLRC individualize consequences under the Labor Code based on status and conduct.

Application: Ramon organized and knowingly led the premature strike. Liza was only an ordinary participant and committed no independently unlawful act.

Conclusion: Ramon's dismissal may be valid; Liza's is not justified on participation alone.
records.Legal Basis / Provision:
Hongkong & Shanghai Banking Corp. Employees Union v. NLRC and CCBPI Postmix Workers Union v. NLRC individualize consequences under the Labor Code based on status and conduct.

Supreme Court E-Library authority: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/61761
records.Controlling Doctrine: Illegal-strike consequences differ: knowing participation may cost a union officer employment, but an ordinary member must have committed an illegal act.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Contracting - LC; D.O. No. 174, s. 2017; Executive Order [E.O.] No. 51; Department Circular No. 1, s. 2017 — Labor-only Contracting
records.Essay Question: Prime Foods hired ServeCo to provide packers. ServeCo was registered and had PHP 5 million paid-up capital, but owned no packing equipment, had no supervisors at the plant, and merely forwarded payroll funds. Prime selected the workers, assigned stations and shifts, prescribed every packing step, evaluated performance, and recommended termination. Prime argues that registration and capitalization conclusively establish legitimate contracting. Is ServeCo a legitimate independent contractor? ServeCo managers visited only to deliver pay envelopes, and Prime supervisors approved leave, imposed daily discipline, and supplied every tool used at the packing stations.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Formal registration and capital do not overcome the absence of an independent business and Prime's control over the workers' methods.

Legal Basis: Labor Code contracting rules and Caballero v. Vikings Commissary look to substantial capital or investment, independent business, and freedom from principal control. Meralco Industrial Engineering also recognizes statutory principal liability in contracting arrangements.

Application: ServeCo supplied labor only, invested no work assets, and exercised no operational control. Prime directed the means and manner of the packers' work.

Conclusion: The arrangement is labor-only contracting, making Prime the direct employer for legal purposes.
records.Legal Basis / Provision:
Labor Code contracting rules and Caballero v. Vikings Commissary look to substantial capital or investment, independent business, and freedom from principal control. Meralco Industrial Engineering also recognizes statutory principal liability in contracting arrangements.

Supreme Court E-Library authority: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68775
records.Controlling Doctrine: Registration and paid-up capital are not conclusive; a contractor that merely supplies labor while the principal controls performance is labor-only.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Termination or Suspension by Employer — Due Process Requirements
records.Essay Question: Employer Delta proved through audit records that cashier Rina deliberately diverted customer payments, a valid just cause. Delta, however, dismissed her through a one-line text message without a notice specifying the accusation or a meaningful chance to answer. Rina claims reinstatement because procedure was ignored. Delta argues that proven cause eliminates every monetary consequence. What is the effect of the procedural breach? The audit trail was authenticated and Rina admits the diversion, so the remaining dispute concerns only whether proven substantive cause eliminates the separate statutory process requirement.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: The dismissal remains valid for proven just cause, but Delta is liable for nominal damages for violating statutory due process.

Legal Basis: King of Kings Transport v. Mamac details the first notice, meaningful opportunity to respond, and decision notice. Agabon v. NLRC holds that proven just cause sustains dismissal despite defective procedure, with PHP 30,000 nominal damages.

Application: The diversion establishes cause, but the text supplied neither specific notice nor an opportunity to defend before decision.

Conclusion: Deny reinstatement and backwages, but award the Agabon nominal damages for the procedural violation.
records.Legal Basis / Provision:
King of Kings Transport v. Mamac details the first notice, meaningful opportunity to respond, and decision notice. Agabon v. NLRC holds that proven just cause sustains dismissal despite defective procedure, with PHP 30,000 nominal damages.

records.Controlling Doctrine: A just-cause dismissal without statutory notice remains substantively valid but exposes the employer to PHP 30,000 nominal damages.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Conditions of Employment — Hours of Work
records.Essay Question: A clinic schedules nurses for eight hours plus a one-hour meal break. During that hour they may leave the premises, turn off work devices, and are never called back. A collective bargaining agreement separately provides two paid ten-minute rest breaks within the eight-hour shift. Nurse Mila claims all sixty meal minutes must also be paid because she remains an employee throughout the day. Is the uninterrupted meal hour compensable working time? During past emergencies, another nurse covered the unit while meal periods continued uninterrupted, confirming that the clinic did not retain a hidden right to recall Mila.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. A genuine uninterrupted meal period during which the employee is fully relieved from duty is ordinarily noncompensable.

Legal Basis: Sime Darby v. NLRC distinguishes an uninterrupted meal period from time spent working or remaining on call. Bonpack v. Nagkakaisang Manggagawa recognizes compensability where shorter breaks are expressly integrated into the workday by agreement.

Application: Mila is free to leave and performs no duty during the full hour. The CBA's separate paid short breaks do not convert the meal hour into work time.

Conclusion: The meal period is noncompensable; the agreed short rest periods remain paid.
records.Legal Basis / Provision:
Sime Darby v. NLRC distinguishes an uninterrupted meal period from time spent working or remaining on call. Bonpack v. Nagkakaisang Manggagawa recognizes compensability where shorter breaks are expressly integrated into the workday by agreement.

Supreme Court E-Library authority: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/35738
records.Controlling Doctrine: A full meal period is noncompensable when the employee is completely relieved from duty, unlike on-call or agreement-integrated short breaks.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Management Prerogative — Transfer of Employees
records.Essay Question: A bank consolidated two nearby branches and transferred teller Juno three kilometers to the surviving branch. Her rank, salary, benefits, schedule, and principal duties remained unchanged. The employer documented that the old branch's lease had ended and offered transportation during transition. Juno refused and claimed constructive dismissal because she preferred her former coworkers. The record shows no discriminatory or punitive motive. Is the transfer unlawful? No replacement employee took Juno former position, and the consolidation memorandum applied the same relocation criteria to all staff assigned at the closed branch.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The transfer is a good-faith business reassignment without demotion, diminution, or unreasonable prejudice.

Legal Basis: Peckson v. Robinsons Supermarket and Mendoza v. Rural Bank of Lucban respect transfers made in good faith for legitimate business needs, while prohibiting discriminatory, punitive, inconvenient, prejudicial, or demotional action.

Application: Branch closure supplies a genuine reason. The short move preserves all material employment terms and includes transition support; personal preference alone does not establish constructive dismissal.

Conclusion: Juno must comply with the lawful transfer.
records.Legal Basis / Provision:
Peckson v. Robinsons Supermarket and Mendoza v. Rural Bank of Lucban respect transfers made in good faith for legitimate business needs, while prohibiting discriminatory, punitive, inconvenient, prejudicial, or demotional action.

Supreme Court E-Library authority: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/56078
records.Controlling Doctrine: Management may transfer an employee for a legitimate business purpose when rank, pay, benefits, and fairness are preserved and no bad faith appears.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Collective Bargaining Agreement — Union Security Clause
records.Essay Question: A collective bargaining agreement contains a valid maintenance-of-membership clause. The union sent employer Apex a one-page demand to dismiss member Sol for alleged nonpayment of dues, attaching no ledger or notice. Apex terminated Sol the same day without asking the union for proof or allowing Sol to answer. Sol produced receipts showing timely payment. Apex says a union demand automatically required dismissal. Was the termination valid? The union treasurer later admitted that the ledger attached to the internal request showed Sol fully paid, but Apex never requested or reviewed that record before dismissal.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The employer had to verify that the clause covered Sol, that the union demand rested on sufficient facts, and that independent due process was observed.

Legal Basis: Alabang Country Club v. NLRC and PICOP Resources v. Tañeca require an applicable security clause, a proper union request, sufficient proof of covered conduct, and fair employer verification.

Application: Apex relied blindly on an unsupported accusation and denied Sol any opportunity to present receipts. The factual basis for invoking the clause was absent.

Conclusion: Sol was illegally dismissed.
records.Legal Basis / Provision:
Alabang Country Club v. NLRC and PICOP Resources v. Tañeca require an applicable security clause, a proper union request, sufficient proof of covered conduct, and fair employer verification.

Supreme Court E-Library authority: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/44870
records.Controlling Doctrine: A union-security demand is not self-executing; the employer must cautiously verify contractual coverage, factual basis, and due process before dismissal.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Kinds of Employment — Fixed Term
records.Essay Question: A food factory hired packer Tess through twenty successive five-month contracts over nine years. The forms were preprinted, offered on a take-it-or-leave-it basis, and covered the same work needed every production day. Management admitted using short terms to avoid regularization and benefits. Tess had no specialized bargaining position and was rehired immediately after each one-day break. The company says each term automatically ended by agreement. Are the fixed terms valid? Each form was prepared solely by management, and workers who requested an indefinite contract were told they would receive no shift at all under the factory policy.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The repeated short terms were imposed to defeat security of tenure and did not reflect a knowingly negotiated agreement on equal footing.

Legal Basis: Pure Foods v. NLRC and Claret School v. Sinday permit genuine fixed-term employment only when knowingly and voluntarily agreed without circumstances vitiating consent or circumventing tenure.

Application: Tess performed permanently necessary work, lacked bargaining equality, and was cycled through identical forms for the admitted purpose of avoiding regular status.

Conclusion: She is a regular employee whose dismissal requires lawful cause and due process.
records.Legal Basis / Provision:
Pure Foods v. NLRC and Claret School v. Sinday permit genuine fixed-term employment only when knowingly and voluntarily agreed without circumstances vitiating consent or circumventing tenure.

Supreme Court E-Library authority: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/35429
records.Controlling Doctrine: A fixed term is invalid when employer-imposed or repeatedly used to circumvent regular employment and security of tenure.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Illegal Recruitment — Distinguished from Estafa - Revised Penal Code, Arts. 315, 316, and 318
records.Essay Question: Unlicensed Mira promised Carlo a hotel job abroad, accepted PHP 90,000 as placement and processing fees, and issued a false deployment schedule. Carlo paid because Mira showed fabricated employer emails. No application was ever submitted and Mira spent the money. She argues that illegal recruitment absorbs estafa because both charges arise from one payment. May she be prosecuted and convicted for both if every element is proved? Carlo preserved the fabricated emails and electronic transfer record, and the licensing authority certified that Mira never held authority during any stage of their dealings.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. Illegal recruitment and estafa are distinct offenses with different elements, even when the same transaction supplies evidence for both.

Legal Basis: People v. Ocden and People v. Valle separately test recruitment activity and absence of license for illegal recruitment, and prior or simultaneous deceit, reliance, and damage for estafa.

Application: Mira undertook recruitment without authority and also used fabricated emails to induce Carlo's payment, causing pecuniary damage. Each offense requires a fact the other does not.

Conclusion: Separate convictions may stand without double jeopardy if all elements are proved beyond reasonable doubt.
records.Legal Basis / Provision:
People v. Ocden and People v. Valle separately test recruitment activity and absence of license for illegal recruitment, and prior or simultaneous deceit, reliance, and damage for estafa.

Supreme Court E-Library authority: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/37842
records.Controlling Doctrine: Illegal recruitment punishes unauthorized recruitment activity; estafa separately punishes deceit causing reliance and damage, so neither necessarily absorbs the other.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Social Security - R.A. No. 11199 — Coverage and Exclusions
records.Essay Question: A Philippine manning agency deploys seafarer Joel to a foreign vessel under a standard overseas contract. The agency argues that Joel is excluded from compulsory SSS coverage because the foreign principal already purchased private life and disability insurance and pays wages abroad. Joel insists that statutory social security and private insurance serve different purposes. Is Joel mandatorily covered, and who bears the contribution responsibilities assigned by law? The agency made no SSS deductions or remittances and relies entirely on the private policy, which names different contingencies and provides no retirement coverage.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. A sea-based overseas Filipino worker remains within compulsory SSS coverage despite private insurance and foreign deployment.

Legal Basis: R.A. No. 11199 expressly governs coverage and contribution allocation. Joint Ship Manning Group v. SSS sustains mandatory coverage of sea-based OFWs and the statutory responsibilities placed on the manning arrangement.

Application: Joel is a deployed sea-based OFW. The foreign principal's private policy supplements rather than replaces the public social-insurance system.

Conclusion: SSS coverage and the law's allocated contribution duties apply.
records.Legal Basis / Provision:
R.A. No. 11199 expressly governs coverage and contribution allocation. Joint Ship Manning Group v. SSS sustains mandatory coverage of sea-based OFWs and the statutory responsibilities placed on the manning arrangement.

records.Controlling Doctrine: Sea-based OFWs are compulsorily covered by the SSS; foreign employment and private insurance do not displace the statutory scheme.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Regional Arbitration Branches (RAB) (Labor Arbiters) — Jurisdiction in Local Employment Cases
records.Essay Question: After engineer Luis resigned, his former employer sued in the Regional Trial Court to recover a training bond based solely on a written reimbursement agreement. The complaint seeks a fixed civil debt and alleges no Labor Code violation, dismissal, wage claim, or unfair labor practice. Luis moves to dismiss, arguing that every dispute arising after employment belongs to the Labor Arbiter. Which forum has jurisdiction? The complaint attaches the bond, payment schedule, and resignation letter and requests no interpretation of workplace standards, disciplinary action, or statutory employee benefit.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: The regular court has jurisdiction because the principal relief is a civil contractual debt without a reasonable causal connection to a labor-law claim.

Legal Basis: Comscentre v. Rocio and Indophil Textile v. Adviento determine jurisdiction from the complaint's allegations, source of obligation, principal relief, and reasonable causal connection, not employee status alone.

Application: The employer invokes an independent reimbursement contract and seeks ordinary debt collection. Resolving it does not require adjudicating rights created by labor law.

Conclusion: The RTC should retain the action, subject to ordinary jurisdictional amount rules.
records.Legal Basis / Provision:
Comscentre v. Rocio and Indophil Textile v. Adviento determine jurisdiction from the complaint's allegations, source of obligation, principal relief, and reasonable causal connection, not employee status alone.

Supreme Court E-Library authority: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/66004
records.Controlling Doctrine: Labor Arbiter jurisdiction depends on the nature and source of the claim and principal relief, not merely the parties' former employment relationship.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Conditions of Employment — Rest Periods
records.Essay Question: A packaging plant's collective bargaining agreement includes two fifteen-minute coffee breaks within the normal eight-hour paid shift. A new supervisor orders employees to clock out for both breaks and extends the shift by thirty minutes without extra pay, saying no work is performed. Workers remain on the premises and must answer line alarms during the breaks. Are the periods compensable? Time records confirm the new thirty-minute extension, and alarm reports identify numerous calls answered during intervals that the supervisor now treats as personal time.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. The agreement integrates the short breaks into the paid workday, and the on-call restriction independently supports compensability.

Legal Basis: Bonpack v. Nagkakaisang Manggagawa enforces CBA-integrated short meal and coffee breaks as part of normal hours. Sime Darby v. NLRC distinguishes a truly uninterrupted meal period from on-call time.

Application: The CBA expressly includes the breaks, and employees remain subject to alarms rather than being completely relieved. The supervisor cannot unilaterally convert them into unpaid extensions.

Conclusion: The thirty minutes remain compensable working time.
records.Legal Basis / Provision:
Bonpack v. Nagkakaisang Manggagawa enforces CBA-integrated short meal and coffee breaks as part of normal hours. Sime Darby v. NLRC distinguishes a truly uninterrupted meal period from on-call time.

Supreme Court E-Library authority: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/35738
records.Controlling Doctrine: Short rest periods integrated by agreement into the workday, especially when employees remain on call, are compensable.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Principles — Equal Pay for Equal Work or Equal Pay for Work of Equal Value
records.Essay Question: A private school pays locally hired and foreign-hired teachers different base salaries. Both groups teach identical subjects, have comparable licenses and experience, carry the same class loads, and work under the same conditions. The school justifies the difference solely by nationality and recruitment origin, while separately reimbursing documented relocation expenses. Local teachers challenge only the lower base salary. Is the salary classification valid? The school supplies no performance metric, seniority rule, or specialized assignment explaining the gap and concedes that local teachers meet the same annual evaluation standards.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Nationality or foreign-hire status alone does not justify unequal base pay for substantially equal work.

Legal Basis: International School Alliance of Educators v. Quisumbing applies equal pay to employees with substantially equal qualifications, skill, effort, responsibility, and working conditions, while allowing genuine distinctions tied to actual circumstances.

Application: The teaching work and qualifications are materially equal. Relocation costs may be separately addressed, but they do not support a permanent nationality-based base-salary gap.

Conclusion: The school must remove the discriminatory base-pay distinction.
records.Legal Basis / Provision:
International School Alliance of Educators v. Quisumbing applies equal pay to employees with substantially equal qualifications, skill, effort, responsibility, and working conditions, while allowing genuine distinctions tied to actual circumstances.

Supreme Court E-Library authority: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/53093
records.Controlling Doctrine: Employees performing substantially equal work under similar conditions must receive equal pay unless a real, job-related distinction justifies differential treatment.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Contracting - LC; D.O. No. 174, s. 2017; Executive Order [E.O.] No. 51; Department Circular No. 1, s. 2017 — Solidary Liability
records.Essay Question: Legitimate contractor BuildPro deployed electricians to MallCo. BuildPro underpaid statutory minimum wages for work performed at the mall, although MallCo paid every invoice in full. The electricians sue both companies. MallCo argues that only a labor-only contracting finding could make it liable and that invoice payment proves good faith. Determine whether MallCo may be solidarily liable for wage deficiencies and whether that result automatically makes it the direct employer for every purpose. Payslips identify BuildPro as employer, while MallCo controlled neither hiring nor daily methods, keeping the wage guarantee distinct from the broader direct-employer question.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: MallCo is solidarily liable for covered unpaid wages even if BuildPro is legitimate, but that limited statutory liability does not by itself make MallCo the direct employer for all purposes.

Legal Basis: Labor Code Articles 106, 107, and 109 and Meralco Industrial Engineering v. NLRC impose indirect-employer solidarity for wages. Labor-only contracting has broader direct-employer consequences.

Application: The claim concerns minimum wages earned on MallCo's project, bringing the statutory wage guarantee into operation. Good-faith invoice payment does not erase worker protection.

Conclusion: Both answer for the deficiency, while broader employment status requires separate analysis.
records.Legal Basis / Provision:
Labor Code Articles 106, 107, and 109 and Meralco Industrial Engineering v. NLRC impose indirect-employer solidarity for wages. Labor-only contracting has broader direct-employer consequences.

Supreme Court E-Library authority: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/44806
records.Controlling Doctrine: A principal is solidarily liable with even a legitimate contractor for covered wage obligations, distinct from the broader effects of labor-only contracting.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Wage Determination - LC, R.A. No. 6727, R.A. No. 8188, R.A. No. 9178, Latest Wage Orders — Wage Distortion
records.Essay Question: A regional wage order raises entry-level wages at a Cebu plant by PHP 60, narrowing the former PHP 70 gap with senior operators to PHP 10. At the employer's Davao plant, management voluntarily gives entry staff a similar raise without any wage order. Senior workers in both plants demand statutory distortion correction. Assess whether the regional setting and source of each increase affect the claims. The Cebu collective agreement preserves defined wage grades, while the Davao agreement contains no corresponding-adjustment clause and has never required parity after voluntary raises.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: The Cebu claim may present statutory wage distortion within one region if the established hierarchy is substantially erased; the voluntary Davao increase does not automatically trigger Article 124's mandatory correction mechanism.

Legal Basis: Prubankers v. Prudential Bank requires a same-region hierarchy, prescribed increase, and elimination or severe contraction of distinctions. Bankard Employees Union v. NLRC holds that a voluntary management increase alone does not activate the statutory mechanism.

Application: Cebu has a wage-order increase and severe contraction within the plant. Davao lacks the prescribed legal increase unless another agreement or practice creates a duty.

Conclusion: Process Cebu under wage-distortion procedures; Davao workers must identify another legal or contractual basis.
records.Legal Basis / Provision:
Prubankers v. Prudential Bank requires a same-region hierarchy, prescribed increase, and elimination or severe contraction of distinctions. Bankard Employees Union v. NLRC holds that a voluntary management increase alone does not activate the statutory mechanism.

Supreme Court E-Library authority: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/29841
records.Controlling Doctrine: Statutory wage distortion requires a prescribed increase that substantially erases an existing same-region hierarchy; a voluntary increase alone does not compel correction.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Termination or Suspension by Employer — Just Causes
records.Essay Question: Warehouse custodian Ben had twice lost high-value packages through careless handling and received written suspensions. He then ignored a mandatory scan procedure and lost another shipment worth PHP 300,000. Separately, he refused a supervisor's order to falsify inventory records. The employer dismisses him for gross and habitual neglect and willful disobedience. Determine which ground is supported. The dismissal notices specify all three grounds separately, and Ben admits the repeated scanning failures but proves that the falsification command violated written compliance policy.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Gross and habitual neglect is supported by the repeated serious failures; willful disobedience is not, because the refused order was unlawful.

Legal Basis: PNB v. Padao defines gross negligence and habitual neglect and recognizes repeated serious loss as just cause. Metro Psychiatry v. Llorente requires the disobeyed order to be reasonable, lawful, known, and work-related.

Application: Three similar losses despite discipline show repeated want of care. Ben was entitled to reject falsification, so that refusal lacks a requisite of insubordination.

Conclusion: Dismissal may rest on proven gross and habitual neglect, subject to due process, but not on the refusal to falsify records.
records.Legal Basis / Provision:
PNB v. Padao defines gross negligence and habitual neglect and recognizes repeated serious loss as just cause. Metro Psychiatry v. Llorente requires the disobeyed order to be reasonable, lawful, known, and work-related.

Supreme Court E-Library authority: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/27251
records.Controlling Doctrine: Just causes are ground-specific: repeated serious carelessness may be gross and habitual neglect, while refusal of an unlawful order is not willful disobedience.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Kinds of Employment — Probationary
records.Essay Question: Clinic Orenda hired therapist Mae on six-month probation and gave her measurable patient-safety and documentation standards on her first day. Monthly evaluations recorded repeated failures. One week before the period ended, Orenda gave written notice terminating her solely for failure to meet those standards, but it did not issue a prior notice to explain or conduct a hearing. Mae argues that she became regular because the full twin-notice procedure was omitted. Were the standards and notice sufficient? Mae received signed copies of the standards and each evaluation, and the termination notice relies on documented nonqualification rather than accusing her of a disciplinary offense.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes, if the standards were reasonable, disclosed at engagement, and genuinely unmet; termination on that sole ground requires timely written notice, not the just-cause twin-notice process.

Legal Basis: Article 296 and Abbott Laboratories v. Alcaraz govern probationary standards and notice. Fixed-term jurisprudence prevents labels from being used to evade tenure but does not erase valid probation.

Application: Orenda disclosed objective standards at hiring, documented failure, and notified Mae before the period ended. No separate misconduct ground triggered just-cause procedure.

Conclusion: The probationary termination is valid on the stated facts.
records.Legal Basis / Provision:
Article 296 and Abbott Laboratories v. Alcaraz govern probationary standards and notice. Fixed-term jurisprudence prevents labels from being used to evade tenure but does not erase valid probation.

Supreme Court E-Library authority: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/69562
records.Controlling Doctrine: A probationary employee may be terminated for failure to meet reasonable standards disclosed at engagement upon proper written notice; just-cause twin notice is not required solely for nonqualification.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Authorized Causes - see also D.O. No. 147, s. 2015 — Disease
records.Essay Question: Hotel Alta dismissed cook Ruel after its private physician reported a treatable skin condition. The report estimated recovery in three months and did not state that continued work was legally prohibited or prejudicial to health. Alta neither sought certification from a competent public health authority nor explored temporary reassignment. It paid separation pay and argues that payment alone validates disease termination. Were the substantive requisites met, and what is the effect of the missing certification? Ruel requested a short medical leave and reassignment away from food preparation, but Alta rejected both options without consulting any public health officer.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Disease termination requires the statutory public-health certification that the illness cannot be cured within six months despite proper treatment and continued employment is prohibited or prejudicial.

Legal Basis: Fuji Television Network v. Espiritu strictly applies the disease ground and competent public-health-authority certification. Medical documentation must establish the statutory conditions, not merely diagnosis.

Application: Alta's private report predicts recovery within three months and omits the required danger finding. Separation pay cannot substitute for substantive cause.

Conclusion: Ruel was illegally dismissed and may claim the appropriate reliefs.
records.Legal Basis / Provision:
Fuji Television Network v. Espiritu strictly applies the disease ground and competent public-health-authority certification. Medical documentation must establish the statutory conditions, not merely diagnosis.

Supreme Court E-Library authority: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/66998
records.Controlling Doctrine: Authorized dismissal for disease requires competent public-health certification of incurability within six months and prejudice from continued employment; payment alone does not cure absence of cause.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Illegal Recruitment — Elements and Types
records.Essay Question: Without a license, Ivo advertised factory jobs abroad, interviewed applicants, collected placement fees, and promised deployment. Four applicants separately paid him after seeing the advertisement. Ivo argues that he merely introduced them to an unknown foreign contact and that the complaints cannot be aggregated because payments occurred on different days. Determine whether recruitment acts occurred and whether the offense may be illegal recruitment in large scale. The Department of Migrant Workers certifies that Ivo held no license, and the four applicants identify the same advertisement, interview location, and promised foreign factory.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. Advertising, canvassing, promising, and collecting fees are recruitment acts; commission against at least three persons by an unlicensed recruiter constitutes large-scale illegal recruitment.

Legal Basis: People v. Liwanag applies the statutory elements and three-victim threshold. People v. Lalli recognizes that referral or facilitation may be recruitment when the accused knowingly performs a pivotal placement role.

Application: Ivo did more than make a casual introduction: he advertised, screened, promised jobs, and took money from four applicants. Separate payment dates do not erase the number of victims.

Conclusion: He may be convicted of illegal recruitment in large scale upon proof beyond reasonable doubt.
records.Legal Basis / Provision:
People v. Liwanag applies the statutory elements and three-victim threshold. People v. Lalli recognizes that referral or facilitation may be recruitment when the accused knowingly performs a pivotal placement role.

Supreme Court E-Library authority: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68333
records.Controlling Doctrine: An unlicensed person who undertakes recruitment acts against three or more victims commits illegal recruitment in large scale.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Liability of Local Recruitment Entity and Foreign Employer — Solidary Liability
records.Essay Question: Local agency Mariner deployed Filipino engineer Bea to a foreign principal under an approved overseas contract. The principal dismissed Bea without cause and withheld three months' salary. Mariner argues that it merely processed papers and that a private side agreement with the principal allocated all worker liabilities abroad. Bea files contract and money claims against both. Are the agency and principal solidarily liable, and can their private allocation defeat Bea's statutory protection? The approved contract names both Mariner and the foreign principal, and the side agreement was never disclosed to Bea before deployment or incorporated into her employment terms.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. The local recruitment agency and foreign principal are solidarily liable for contract-based overseas employment claims; their private allocation cannot prejudice the worker.

Legal Basis: R.A. No. 8042 and Sameer Overseas Placement Agency v. Cabiles impose solidary responsibility to secure effective recovery by deployed workers. Labor Arbiter jurisdiction covers qualifying overseas contract claims.

Application: Bea's unpaid wages and illegal termination arise directly from the approved deployment contract. Mariner participated as the licensed local agency and cannot contract away the statutory guarantee against her.

Conclusion: Bea may recover the lawful award from either or both, without prejudice to their internal reimbursement rights.
records.Legal Basis / Provision:
R.A. No. 8042 and Sameer Overseas Placement Agency v. Cabiles impose solidary responsibility to secure effective recovery by deployed workers. Labor Arbiter jurisdiction covers qualifying overseas contract claims.

Supreme Court E-Library authority: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/57319
records.Controlling Doctrine: The local agency and foreign principal are solidarily liable for covered overseas employment claims, and private allocation cannot diminish the worker's remedy.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Unfair Labor Practice — By Employers
records.Essay Question: Company Orion gives a meal allowance only to employees holding accounting degrees, regardless of union membership. The union calls the distinction unfair labor practice. In a separate act, Orion refuses for six months to meet the duly certified bargaining representative despite repeated written demands and offers no justification. Determine whether each act is employer unfair labor practice. The allowance policy predates union organization and applies to all degree holders, while bargaining receipts establish that authorized company officers received every unanswered demand.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: The degree-based allowance is not ULP absent a link to self-organization, though it may raise other issues; the unjustified refusal to bargain with the certified representative may be ULP.

Legal Basis: AIM Faculty Association v. AIM explains that an act is not ULP merely because unfair; it must violate organizational or bargaining rights. Ren Transport v. NLRC recognizes the duty to bargain with the certified representative.

Application: The allowance classification is neutral as to union activity on the stated facts. The prolonged refusal directly obstructs the statutory bargaining right.

Conclusion: Reject the first ULP charge but sustain the second upon proof of certification and unjustified refusal.
records.Legal Basis / Provision:
AIM Faculty Association v. AIM explains that an act is not ULP merely because unfair; it must violate organizational or bargaining rights. Ren Transport v. NLRC recognizes the duty to bargain with the certified representative.

Supreme Court E-Library authority: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/67502
records.Controlling Doctrine: Employer ULP requires interference with self-organization or bargaining rights; ordinary unfairness alone is insufficient, while unjustified refusal to bargain may qualify.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Peaceful Concerted Activities - see also R.A. No. 6727 — Assumption of Jurisdiction by DOLE Secretary
records.Essay Question: Nurses at the region's only trauma hospital declared a strike during a bargaining deadlock. Before the scheduled stoppage, the Labor Secretary assumed jurisdiction over the dispute and directed employees to remain at work. The union received the order but proceeded, arguing that its strike vote and notices were otherwise complete. The hospital then refused to readmit every participant. What is the effect of the assumption order, and are dismissal consequences automatic for all workers? The Secretary order cites the hospital regional trauma role and directs immediate maintenance of operations, and union officers personally received copies before the scheduled walkout.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: The assumption order automatically enjoins the strike and requires compliance, but employment consequences still depend on each worker's status, knowledge, and conduct under governing rules.

Legal Basis: San Pedro Hospital v. Secretary of Labor gives an assumption or certification order immediate return-to-work effect in an industry indispensable to national interest. Illegal-strike jurisprudence individualizes dismissal consequences.

Application: A trauma hospital supports the national-interest intervention, and receipt made the continued strike defiant. Yet the hospital cannot treat officers and ordinary members identically without proof required for each.

Conclusion: The strike after the order was prohibited; adjudicate individual sanctions rather than impose blanket dismissal.
records.Legal Basis / Provision:
San Pedro Hospital v. Secretary of Labor gives an assumption or certification order immediate return-to-work effect in an industry indispensable to national interest. Illegal-strike jurisprudence individualizes dismissal consequences.

Supreme Court E-Library authority: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/34165
records.Controlling Doctrine: Assumption of jurisdiction immediately enjoins a strike and commands return to work, while disciplinary consequences remain individualized.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Regional Arbitration Branches (RAB) (Labor Arbiters) — Jurisdiction in Overseas Employment Cases - R.A. No. 8042
records.Essay Question: Philippine agency Seaway deployed Lea to a foreign hotel under an approved contract. After termination, Lea filed before a Labor Arbiter for unpaid salaries and damages against Seaway and the foreign principal. Seaway argues that the work occurred abroad and that the foreign principal is beyond Philippine labor jurisdiction. Lea relies on the overseas-employment contract and statutory solidarity. Does the Labor Arbiter have subject-matter jurisdiction, and may the local agency be held for the award? The deployment contract identifies Seaway as the local agency and states the foreign hotel position, salary, and termination terms that Lea asks the tribunal to enforce.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Yes. The Labor Arbiter may hear money and termination claims arising from an overseas employment contract, and the local agency may be solidarily liable with the foreign principal.

Legal Basis: R.A. No. 8042, Sameer Overseas v. Cabiles, and Lamadrid v. Cathay Pacific recognize Philippine labor adjudication of qualifying overseas employment claims and effective recovery against responsible entities.

Application: Lea's claims arise directly from the approved deployment contract, not a separate civil transaction. Seaway's local participation and statutory solidarity provide an enforceable respondent.

Conclusion: The Labor Arbiter should take jurisdiction and adjudicate both respondents' liability.
records.Legal Basis / Provision:
R.A. No. 8042, Sameer Overseas v. Cabiles, and Lamadrid v. Cathay Pacific recognize Philippine labor adjudication of qualifying overseas employment claims and effective recovery against responsible entities.

Supreme Court E-Library authority: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/67427
records.Controlling Doctrine: Labor Arbiters have jurisdiction over covered overseas employment contract claims, with local recruitment agencies solidarily answerable alongside foreign principals.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Employer-Employee Relationship — Tests
records.Essay Question: Freelance architect Pia accepts projects from many clients, advertises her own studio, negotiates each fee, chooses assistants and software, sets her schedule, may decline assignments, and bears profit or loss. Developer Hexa specifies only required drawings, safety codes, and completion dates. Hexa pays by milestone and cannot discipline Pia, although it may reject noncompliant results. Pia later claims employee status because Hexa reviewed plans weekly and its projects supplied forty percent of her income. Does result-oriented review establish an employment relationship?
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The facts show an independent business and client control over results, not the means and methods of Pia's professional work.

Legal Basis: Ditiangkin v. Lazada and Gaspar v. M.I.Y. Real Estate distinguish the right to control work methods from specifications of desired results. Economic dependence is contextual and does not replace a sufficient control analysis.

Application: Pia serves multiple clients, controls performance, hires help, negotiates fees, and bears entrepreneurial risk. Weekly compliance review protects the desired output only.

Conclusion: Pia is an independent contractor on the stated facts.
records.Legal Basis / Provision:
Ditiangkin v. Lazada and Gaspar v. M.I.Y. Real Estate distinguish the right to control work methods from specifications of desired results. Economic dependence is contextual and does not replace a sufficient control analysis.

Supreme Court E-Library authority: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68763
records.Controlling Doctrine: Client specifications and quality review do not create employment when an independent professional controls work methods and operates a genuine separate business.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Termination or Suspension by Employer — Constructive Dismissal v. Demotion
records.Essay Question: Because its main office was flooded, firm Nova temporarily transferred accountant Leo to a nearby branch for six weeks. His rank, pay, benefits, hours, and accounting duties remained identical; the firm paid additional transport costs and documented the restoration schedule. Leo resigned on the first day and alleged constructive dismissal, relying only on the inconvenience of a thirty-minute longer commute. Does every inconvenient transfer amount to constructive dismissal? Branch records confirm that no benefit changed and every displaced employee received the same temporary arrangement, while the restoration contractor expects the main office to reopen on schedule.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. A temporary, good-faith transfer for a genuine operational need, with equivalent terms and reasonable support, is within management prerogative.

Legal Basis: Emirate Security v. Menese and Automatic Appliances v. Deguidoy condemn transfers that are demotional, discriminatory, punitive, or unreasonably prejudicial, not every reassignment causing some inconvenience.

Application: The flood is a legitimate reason, all material terms remain intact, duration is fixed, and transport is covered. The additional commute alone is not objectively intolerable.

Conclusion: Leo voluntarily resigned and was not constructively dismissed on these facts.
records.Legal Basis / Provision:
Emirate Security v. Menese and Automatic Appliances v. Deguidoy condemn transfers that are demotional, discriminatory, punitive, or unreasonably prejudicial, not every reassignment causing some inconvenience.

Supreme Court E-Library authority: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/26790
records.Controlling Doctrine: Constructive dismissal requires objectively unreasonable or prejudicial change; ordinary inconvenience from a justified equivalent transfer is insufficient.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Principles — Non-diminution of Benefits
records.Essay Question: For five years, Solara announced a “profit-sharing bonus” each March. Written notices stated that the board could grant nothing, that amounts depended on audited profits and individual ratings, and that no payment created a future entitlement. Employees received varying sums in three profitable years and none in two loss years. When another loss year produced no bonus, they claim a protected company practice based on repeated payments. Has the bonus become nondiminishable? Audited statements confirm the current loss, and no individual rating or board resolution grants a payment for this year under the written program.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. The grant remained expressly discretionary and contingent on profits and performance rather than fixed, deliberate, and unconditional.

Legal Basis: Arco Metal v. Samahan and Producers Bank v. NLRC distinguish established regular benefits from bonuses tied to profit, performance, or continuing management discretion.

Application: The written reservations were repeated, amounts varied, and nonpayment already occurred in loss years. The pattern confirms the condition instead of contradicting it.

Conclusion: Article 100 does not compel a bonus for the current loss year.
records.Legal Basis / Provision:
Arco Metal v. Samahan and Producers Bank v. NLRC distinguish established regular benefits from bonuses tied to profit, performance, or continuing management discretion.

Supreme Court E-Library authority: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/45241
records.Controlling Doctrine: A genuinely discretionary, profit-contingent bonus does not become an established benefit merely because it was paid in several profitable years.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Peaceful Concerted Activities - see also R.A. No. 6727 — Strikes
records.Essay Question: During an otherwise lawful strike, ordinary union member Ena remained on the public sidewalk, carried a placard, obeyed police lines, and committed no coercion or damage. A different group blocked the gate and vandalized vehicles. The employer dismissed every participant, arguing that any ordinary member who joins a strike loses employment once someone commits an unlawful act. Can Ena be dismissed on participation alone? Police video shows Ena repeatedly stepping away from the blocked gate and asking other picketers to keep the public entrance open for emergency vehicles.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. An ordinary union member in a strike requires proof that she personally committed an illegal act before dismissal is justified on that basis.

Legal Basis: HSBC Employees Union v. NLRC and CCBPI Postmix Workers Union v. NLRC distinguish union officers' knowing participation in an illegal strike from ordinary members' individual unlawful acts.

Application: Ena's conduct was peaceful and no evidence connects her to obstruction or vandalism. Other members' acts cannot automatically be imputed to her.

Conclusion: Ena's dismissal is invalid absent proof of her own illegal act or another lawful cause.
records.Legal Basis / Provision:
HSBC Employees Union v. NLRC and CCBPI Postmix Workers Union v. NLRC distinguish union officers' knowing participation in an illegal strike from ordinary members' individual unlawful acts.

Supreme Court E-Library authority: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/61761
records.Controlling Doctrine: An ordinary strike participant is not dismissible through collective attribution; the employer must prove that the member personally committed an illegal act.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Contracting - LC; D.O. No. 174, s. 2017; Executive Order [E.O.] No. 51; Department Circular No. 1, s. 2017 — Labor-only Contracting
records.Essay Question: CleanTech contracts to maintain a semiconductor plant. It owns specialized machines worth PHP 20 million, employs its own engineers and supervisors, sets work methods, hires and disciplines staff, serves several clients, and bears project profit or loss. PlantCo specifies cleanliness results and safety protocols but does not direct daily means. Workers argue that because maintenance is necessary to PlantCo's business, contracting must be labor-only. Is necessity of the work alone decisive? CleanTech invoices clients under its own name, maintains separate insurance, and can replace assigned engineers without PlantCo approval so long as safety credentials remain satisfied.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. Necessary or desirable work does not by itself establish labor-only contracting when the contractor operates an independent, substantially equipped business free from control over methods.

Legal Basis: Contracting law examines independent business, capital or investment, and control. Caballero v. Vikings Commissary addresses labor-only consequences, while Meralco Industrial Engineering distinguishes legitimate contracting from statutory wage solidarity.

Application: CleanTech supplies substantial equipment, expertise, supervision, multiple-client operations, and entrepreneurial risk. PlantCo controls results and safety, not performance methods.

Conclusion: The arrangement is legitimate contracting on the stated facts.
records.Legal Basis / Provision:
Contracting law examines independent business, capital or investment, and control. Caballero v. Vikings Commissary addresses labor-only consequences, while Meralco Industrial Engineering distinguishes legitimate contracting from statutory wage solidarity.

Supreme Court E-Library authority: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/68775
records.Controlling Doctrine: Performance of necessary work is not conclusive of labor-only contracting when a substantially capitalized independent contractor controls the means and manner of work.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Termination or Suspension by Employer — Due Process Requirements
records.Essay Question: Employer Rho served worker Sami a detailed first notice identifying dates, transactions, witnesses, and the charged just cause. Sami received ten calendar days to submit documents and requested no conference. After considering his written explanation, Rho issued a reasoned decision notice. Sami argues that dismissal is procedurally void because no face-to-face hearing occurred. The company proves that Sami had access to the evidence and a meaningful written opportunity to answer. Is a formal trial-type hearing invariably required? Sami response addressed every listed transaction and attached countervailing documents, which the final notice summarized and evaluated before explaining why management rejected them.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. A meaningful opportunity to be heard may be satisfied through adequate written notice and response unless a conference is requested or material factual disputes require one.

Legal Basis: King of Kings Transport v. Mamac requires specific notice, reasonable opportunity to answer, and a reasoned decision, but does not make a courtroom hearing indispensable in every case. Agabon supplies consequences for actual procedural breach.

Application: Sami knew the precise accusations, had sufficient time and evidence, answered in writing, and did not seek a conference.

Conclusion: The stated procedure satisfies statutory due process.
records.Legal Basis / Provision:

records.Controlling Doctrine: Labor due process requires a real opportunity to answer, not invariably an oral trial, when detailed notice and meaningful written response are afforded.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Conditions of Employment — Hours of Work
records.Essay Question: A call center labels a sixty-minute interval as “meal break,” but agents must remain logged in, answer priority calls within thirty seconds, and obtain permission even to leave their desks. Records show most agents handle four to six calls during each interval. The employer argues that any break scheduled for sixty minutes is automatically noncompensable. Does the nominal duration control? Call logs and screen recordings match the agents accounts, and payroll deducted the interval even on days when priority traffic occupied most of the scheduled hour.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: No. A meal period is noncompensable only when the employee is completely relieved from duty; substantial on-call restrictions make the time compensable.

Legal Basis: Sime Darby v. NLRC focuses on whether the meal period is genuinely uninterrupted and duty-free. Bonpack v. Nagkakaisang Manggagawa recognizes compensability of breaks integrated into the working day.

Application: Agents remain at their stations, must respond immediately, and regularly perform calls. The employer controls the period for its benefit despite the label and scheduled length.

Conclusion: The entire on-call meal interval is compensable working time.
records.Legal Basis / Provision:
Sime Darby v. NLRC focuses on whether the meal period is genuinely uninterrupted and duty-free. Bonpack v. Nagkakaisang Manggagawa recognizes compensability of breaks integrated into the working day.

Supreme Court E-Library authority: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/35738
records.Controlling Doctrine: The actual duty and control during a break, not its label or nominal length, determine compensability.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Management Prerogative — Transfer of Employees
records.Essay Question: Supervisor Mina is transferred from Manila to a distant island branch after testifying against an executive. Her title is retained, but her supervisory staff, housing allowance, and decision authority are removed. The company gives no operational reason and orders her to report in forty-eight hours. Mina files a constructive-dismissal complaint. What factual burdens should the parties address, and what relief follows if the transfer is shown punitive and prejudicial? A branch vacancy existed before Mina testimony, but management filled it with another supervisor and created a lower-authority assignment for her only after the executive complaint.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: The employer must substantiate a legitimate good-faith business reason, while Mina must show material prejudice or bad faith; a proven punitive demotion supports constructive-dismissal relief.

Legal Basis: Peckson v. Robinsons Supermarket and Mendoza v. Rural Bank of Lucban set the transfer limits of equivalent rank and pay, business necessity, good faith, and absence of unreasonable prejudice.

Application: The timing, lost authority and allowance, extreme relocation, and unexplained urgency support punishment rather than genuine deployment. The employer's bare prerogative claim is insufficient.

Conclusion: If these facts are proved, award the statutory remedies for constructive dismissal.
records.Legal Basis / Provision:
Peckson v. Robinsons Supermarket and Mendoza v. Rural Bank of Lucban set the transfer limits of equivalent rank and pay, business necessity, good faith, and absence of unreasonable prejudice.

Supreme Court E-Library authority: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/56078
records.Controlling Doctrine: A transfer challenged as constructive dismissal requires evidence of business purpose and actual consequences; punitive or demotional reassignment warrants labor remedies.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Collective Bargaining Agreement — Union Security Clause
records.Essay Question: Union Unity asks employer Ferro to dismiss three workers under a union-security clause. The demand identifies the clause and alleged resignation from the union but attaches no membership records. Before acting, Ferro wants a defensible procedure that respects the collective agreement and employee due process. What steps should it take, and may it suspend final action while verifying the demand? The collective agreement defines resignation from membership, and one worker says the signature attributed to her was forged, making source records and an individual response essential.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Ferro should confirm clause coverage and validity, require a factually supported union demand, give each worker specific notice and a meaningful chance to respond, independently evaluate the evidence, and issue a reasoned decision; verification before dismissal is proper.

Legal Basis: Alabang Country Club v. NLRC and PICOP Resources v. Tañeca require applicable contractual coverage, proper union request, sufficient proof, and independent employer fairness.

Application: The unsupported demand leaves membership status and covered conduct uncertain. Immediate dismissal would substitute union assertion for employer judgment and deny the workers a defense.

Conclusion: Pause final action, gather records, hear both sides, and enforce the clause only if every requisite is proved.
records.Legal Basis / Provision:
Alabang Country Club v. NLRC and PICOP Resources v. Tañeca require applicable contractual coverage, proper union request, sufficient proof, and independent employer fairness.

Supreme Court E-Library authority: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/44870
records.Controlling Doctrine: A prudent employer treats union-security dismissal as an evidence-based due-process decision, not a ministerial response to the union's request.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Kinds of Employment — Fixed Term
records.Essay Question: Lecturer Omi and a university, represented by separate counsel, negotiated a one-year appointment for a single externally funded research project. The written term matched the grant, described the project endpoint, preserved statutory benefits, and was not renewed after funding ended. Omi later files for illegal dismissal, alleging regular work. What evidence should the tribunal examine to decide whether the fixed term was genuine, and what result follows if equal bargaining and project linkage are proved? The grant agreement ends automatically after twelve months, and the university has no comparable permanent project or successor funding available after the research deliverables are accepted.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: The tribunal should examine informed voluntary consent, bargaining equality, the objective project endpoint, work necessity, repeated renewals, and any tenure-avoidance purpose; a genuinely negotiated grant-linked term may validly expire.

Legal Basis: Pure Foods v. NLRC and Claret School v. Sinday enforce fixed terms only when knowingly and voluntarily agreed on relatively equal footing and not designed to defeat security of tenure.

Application: Separate counsel, a specific one-year grant, clear endpoint, and preserved benefits indicate a real term rather than employer-imposed cycling.

Conclusion: If those facts are established, expiration ends the appointment without illegal dismissal.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Illegal Recruitment — Distinguished from Estafa - Revised Penal Code, Arts. 315, 316, and 318
records.Essay Question: A prosecutor receives complaints that unlicensed recruiter Zed promised foreign jobs to five applicants, collected fees, and used fabricated visas. The applicants' affidavits and receipts cover both unauthorized recruitment and deceit. Zed asks the prosecutor to choose only one charge to avoid duplicative prosecution. How should the informations and evidence be organized without treating the offenses as identical? Each applicant can identify a distinct false visa and payment, while the licensing certification and common advertisement link all five recruitment transactions to Zed.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: The prosecutor may file the proper illegal-recruitment charge and separate estafa counts, pleading and proving each offense's distinct elements and victim-specific deceit and damage.

Legal Basis: People v. Ocden and People v. Valle distinguish the recruitment-license and recruitment-act elements from estafa's false representation, reliance, and pecuniary injury.

Application: The five-victim scheme may support large-scale recruitment, while each fabricated visa and induced payment may establish a separate deceit offense. Shared evidence does not merge distinct elements.

Conclusion: Charge distinctly, avoid duplicative factual allegations where unnecessary, and prove every statutory element independently.
records.Legal Basis / Provision:
People v. Ocden and People v. Valle distinguish the recruitment-license and recruitment-act elements from estafa's false representation, reliance, and pecuniary injury.

Supreme Court E-Library authority: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/37842
records.Controlling Doctrine: Proper prosecution separates unauthorized recruitment from victim-specific estafa even when the same scheme and payments supply overlapping evidence.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Social Security - R.A. No. 11199 — Coverage and Exclusions
records.Essay Question: A manning agency refuses to register its deployed seafarers with SSS, asserting that foreign principals already insure them. Seafarer Lina seeks practical relief before disability arises. What official records and employment documents should she present, and what relief may she request to enforce statutory coverage and contributions? Lina has copies of her seafarer contract, allotment slips, passport deployment stamps, private policy, and an SSS printout showing no posted contribution during three completed voyages. The agency remains licensed and continues deploying her crewmates under identical arrangements.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Lina should present her deployment contract, agency and principal details, payroll, seafarer status, and contribution history, and seek SSS enforcement of compulsory registration, correct contribution allocation, and posting of arrears under R.A. No. 11199.

Legal Basis: R.A. No. 11199 establishes compulsory coverage and administrative enforcement. Joint Ship Manning Group v. SSS confirms application to sea-based OFWs despite private insurance and foreign principals.

Application: The agency's private coverage argument does not satisfy the public system. The records establish the covered relationship, compensation base, and missing remittances for an enforceable account correction.

Conclusion: SSS should require coverage and lawful contribution compliance without waiting for a benefit contingency.
records.Legal Basis / Provision:
R.A. No. 11199 establishes compulsory coverage and administrative enforcement. Joint Ship Manning Group v. SSS confirms application to sea-based OFWs despite private insurance and foreign principals.

Supreme Court E-Library authority: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/2/86333
records.Controlling Doctrine: Compulsory SSS coverage is enforceable prospectively through registration and contribution correction; private insurance is no substitute.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Regional Arbitration Branches (RAB) (Labor Arbiters) — Jurisdiction in Local Employment Cases
records.Essay Question: Employee Kira files before a Labor Arbiter seeking unpaid wages and damages for retaliatory dismissal. Her former employer counterclaims for return of a company laptop and payment under an unrelated personal car loan signed years before employment. The employer argues that the Labor Arbiter may decide every dispute between the parties to avoid multiplicity of suits. How should jurisdiction be separated, and what claims belong in the labor case? The laptop was issued under a signed accountability form and remains necessary to complete final payroll clearance, while the car loan predates hiring and names no employment consequence.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: The Labor Arbiter may decide employment claims and counterclaims reasonably connected to the employment relationship, but the independent personal loan belongs to the regular courts; return of company property may be addressed if sufficiently connected to employment relief.

Legal Basis: Comscentre v. Rocio and Indophil Textile v. Adviento examine allegations, principal relief, source of obligation, and reasonable causal connection rather than party identity alone.

Application: Wages, dismissal, and work-issued equipment arise from employment. The old personal car loan rests on an independent civil contract unrelated to labor rights.

Conclusion: Retain the labor-connected matters and dismiss or sever the personal debt without prejudice to a civil action.
records.Legal Basis / Provision:
Comscentre v. Rocio and Indophil Textile v. Adviento examine allegations, principal relief, source of obligation, and reasonable causal connection rather than party identity alone.

Supreme Court E-Library authority: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/66004
records.Controlling Doctrine: Labor jurisdiction is claim-specific; tribunals separate employment-connected relief from independent civil obligations even between the same parties.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Conditions of Employment — Rest Periods
records.Essay Question: Workers claim two daily fifteen-minute rest periods were unlawfully removed from paid time. The employer's electronic records show clock-outs, but the collective bargaining agreement states that both breaks are included in the normal eight-hour day, and alarm logs show workers were repeatedly recalled. Before computing an award, what evidence should the Labor Arbiter compare, and how should compensable time be determined? The union also preserved negotiation minutes showing that paid integration of the breaks was exchanged for a different scheduling concession during the last bargaining cycle.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: The arbiter should compare the CBA, schedules, time logs, recall records, actual restrictions, payroll computations, and representative testimony, then count breaks contractually integrated or spent predominantly for the employer as working time.

Legal Basis: Bonpack v. Nagkakaisang Manggagawa treats CBA-integrated short breaks as compensable. Sime Darby v. NLRC distinguishes fully relieved meal periods from on-call time.

Application: Clock-out labels do not defeat the express CBA or actual recall evidence. Damages should be computed from proven affected days and applicable premiums, avoiding unsupported blanket estimates.

Conclusion: Recognize compensable breaks and order a record-based payroll recomputation.
records.Legal Basis / Provision:
Bonpack v. Nagkakaisang Manggagawa treats CBA-integrated short breaks as compensable. Sime Darby v. NLRC distinguishes fully relieved meal periods from on-call time.

Supreme Court E-Library authority: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/35738
records.Controlling Doctrine: Rest-period claims require examination of both governing agreement and actual control; time records cannot override proved on-call work or CBA integration.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Principles — Equal Pay for Equal Work or Equal Pay for Work of Equal Value
records.Essay Question: Women quality inspectors allege that male inspectors receive twenty percent higher base pay. Job descriptions are identical, but the employer asserts that men perform heavier work and have greater responsibility. The employer produces only titles and a generalized affidavit; employees submit schedules, evaluation forms, and output records showing equal tasks and qualifications. What comparative evidence should the tribunal assess, and who must justify the differential after substantial equality is shown? The schedules assign both groups to the same inspection lines and hazards, and annual evaluations use a common competency matrix with no heavier-work category.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: The tribunal should compare actual skill, effort, responsibility, qualifications, and working conditions, not titles; once substantial equality and a pay gap are shown, the employer must identify and prove a genuine nondiscriminatory basis.

Legal Basis: International School Alliance of Educators v. Quisumbing applies equal pay for substantially equal work and rejects distinctions unsupported by real differences. Dela Cruz-Cagampan scrutinizes sex-based employment policies and business-necessity claims.

Application: The employees' operational records contradict the bare assertion of heavier work. Without task-specific proof, sex-correlated pay lacks a legitimate basis.

Conclusion: Order equalization and proven wage differentials if the employer cannot substantiate its defense.
records.Legal Basis / Provision:
International School Alliance of Educators v. Quisumbing applies equal pay for substantially equal work and rejects distinctions unsupported by real differences. Dela Cruz-Cagampan scrutinizes sex-based employment policies and business-necessity claims.

Supreme Court E-Library authority: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/53093
records.Controlling Doctrine: Equal-pay adjudication compares actual work and conditions; labels or generalized claims cannot justify a material differential after substantial equality is proved.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Contracting - LC; D.O. No. 174, s. 2017; Executive Order [E.O.] No. 51; Department Circular No. 1, s. 2017 — Solidary Liability
records.Essay Question: Compare two consequences of contracting. In Arrangement A, a genuinely independent contractor underpays statutory wages to workers deployed at the principal's project. In Arrangement B, a sham contractor merely supplies labor while the principal controls every work method. The principal argues that liability is identical in both and never affects employer status. Classify the principal's liability and relationship in each arrangement. In both arrangements the same wage shortage is proved, but only the sham contractor lacks equipment, supervisors, outside clients, and independent control over performance.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: In A, the principal has limited statutory solidary liability for covered wages despite legitimate contracting. In B, labor-only contracting makes the principal the direct employer, with broader labor obligations.

Legal Basis: Meralco Industrial Engineering v. NLRC explains indirect-employer wage solidarity even with a legitimate contractor. Caballero v. Vikings Commissary applies the direct-employer consequences of labor-only contracting.

Application: A preserves the contractor's independent employer role while guaranteeing wages. B lacks genuine independence and shifts employer status to the principal by law.

Conclusion: Apply limited wage solidarity to A and direct-employer liability to B.
records.Legal Basis / Provision:
Meralco Industrial Engineering v. NLRC explains indirect-employer wage solidarity even with a legitimate contractor. Caballero v. Vikings Commissary applies the direct-employer consequences of labor-only contracting.

Supreme Court E-Library authority: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/44806
records.Controlling Doctrine: Legitimate contracting creates a targeted wage guarantee; labor-only contracting creates a direct employment relationship and broader liability.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Wage Determination - LC, R.A. No. 6727, R.A. No. 8188, R.A. No. 9178, Latest Wage Orders — Wage Distortion
records.Essay Question: Plant East receives a mandatory regional wage-order increase that nearly eliminates the gap between junior and senior grades in the same establishment. Plant West, in another region, receives no wage order, but the employer voluntarily grants junior workers a matching raise. Senior workers at both plants invoke Article 124. Classify the two situations and identify which enters the statutory wage-distortion mechanism. Neither plant has a contractual parity clause, and the comparison concerns the statutory correction process rather than any independently negotiated promise to maintain fixed ratios.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: Plant East may present statutory wage distortion because a prescribed same-region increase severely contracts an established hierarchy; Plant West's voluntary increase does not automatically enter Article 124.

Legal Basis: Prubankers v. Prudential Bank identifies the prescribed increase, same-region hierarchy, and severe contraction elements. Bankard Employees Union v. NLRC distinguishes voluntary management adjustments.

Application: East has the statutory trigger and structural effect. West lacks a wage-order source, although a CBA or established practice might create a separate obligation.

Conclusion: Use Article 124 procedures for East and require an independent legal basis for West.
records.Legal Basis / Provision:
Prubankers v. Prudential Bank identifies the prescribed increase, same-region hierarchy, and severe contraction elements. Bankard Employees Union v. NLRC distinguishes voluntary management adjustments.

Supreme Court E-Library authority: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/29841
records.Controlling Doctrine: Wage-order distortion and management-created compression may look similar economically but differ legally because only the prescribed increase automatically triggers Article 124.

records.Subject: Labor Law
records.Topic: Termination or Suspension by Employer — Just Causes
records.Essay Question: Employee A mistakenly misfiles one report, promptly corrects it, and has a clean ten-year record. Employee B repeatedly ignores a safety checklist after two warnings, causing three costly shutdowns. Employee C deliberately refuses an instruction to conceal a chemical spill from regulators. The employer labels all three “gross neglect or willful disobedience.” Classify the conduct under just-cause standards. The personnel files provide prior warnings and loss reports for B, no discipline for A, and a written environmental policy expressly prohibiting the concealment demanded from C.
records.Suggested Answer:
Answer: A's isolated minor mistake is not gross and habitual neglect; B's repeated serious failures may be; C's refusal is not willful disobedience because the order was unlawful.

Legal Basis: PNB v. Padao requires serious want of care and repetition for gross and habitual neglect. Metro Psychiatry v. Llorente requires a disobeyed order to be lawful, reasonable, known, and connected to duties.

Application: A lacks gravity and habit. B shows repeated neglect despite warnings and material harm. C properly rejected an unlawful concealment directive.

Conclusion: Only B's conduct supports the asserted just cause, subject to proportionality and due process.
records.Legal Basis / Provision:
PNB v. Padao requires serious want of care and repetition for gross and habitual neglect. Metro Psychiatry v. Llorente requires a disobeyed order to be lawful, reasonable, known, and connected to duties.

Supreme Court E-Library authority: https://elibrary.judiciary.gov.ph/thebookshelf/showdocs/1/27251
records.Controlling Doctrine: Just-cause classification turns on gravity, repetition, and legality of the order, not the employer's chosen label.
